I’m sitting on a barstool at the back of a crowded rooftop, taking notes on a pitch I can’t follow, when I hear the word “traction” and look up. 

The first of five founders is at the mic, making his way through a pitch deck. 

Since I can’t really see the stage from where I’m sitting, my eyes stay on the page where I’m taking notes. 

Up until this point, all I have jotted down is “Confident presence”. I heard the term “real estate” and then some other words strung together in a way that made no sense to me. If I were in real estate, I’m sure they still wouldn’t. But I kept listening. 

We were several slides in and I still didn’t know what pain point or problem he was solving. At the time of writing, I still couldn’t tell you. It was that unmemorable. 

But then he mentions their traction. Impressive, real numbers from real customers. And they’ve just raised $2M. I look up and catch a glimpse of the slide. He’s a Y Combinator founder from a previous startup. "Impressive", I think to myself.

Thank you to Neethu Stephen, Founder of Evalua8 and co-founder of Startup Roundtable, for yesterday's guest lecture on #EntrepreneurialFinance for our #EntrepreneurshipandBusinessVentures students at Bournemouth University Business School.

Finance is rarely the part of entrepreneurship that students rush towards. Neethu changed that with "The Founder's Board", a monopoly-style board-game framework that places the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement on one board, with the founder's levers (pricing, forecasting, budgeting, KPIs, fundraising and scaling) running alongside them. 

The format made one point impossible to miss: financial statements don't exist separately. A single founder decision moves several squares at once.

Her "myths busted" section was a highlight. "We're profitable, so we're fine" didn't survive the session, and anyone who had quietly earmarked the VAT for something nice learned it belonged to HMRC all along.

Neethu took working capital, burn rate and runway, which sound drier than they are, and made them clear, practical and genuinely enjoyable. As a result, our students are better equipped to develop and pitch their own ventures.

Thank you, Neethu, for your time, generosity and expertise. Nobody went to #monopoly jail, though several bad assumptions did.

If we look beyond the logo, what do we find?

A lot more than most people expect.

When I think about a brand, I see five interconnected areas:

1️⃣ Strategy: the thinking that gives the brand direction. It answers who the brand is for, what it stands for, and why it exists.

2️⃣ Visual identity: the logo, colour, typography, and imagery that represent the brand and make it recognisable.

3️⃣ Messaging: how the brand communicates. This covers its tone, language, and the stories it tells.

4️⃣ Experience: how people interact with the brand at every touchpoint, from the first impression to the last.

5️⃣ Perception: how people come to understand the brand and what they associate with it.

None of these works well alone.

A visual identity should support the brand’s positioning. Messaging should reflect its personality. The customer experience should reinforce the promises the brand makes.

When one area drifts from the others, people feel it. They may not be able to explain why, but the brand seems inconsistent, and trust is harder to build.

This is why I find branding so interesting. It isn’t about producing a logo, then a website, then a social media post, each as a separate task. It’s about thinking in systems and making sure every output pulls in the same direction.

A logo is just one visible expression of a much bigger idea.

Which of these five areas do you think businesses overlook the most? I’d love to hear your take. 👇

The UK wants to become a global hub for innovation. But apparently, there's one problem: startups behave like startups.

They take risks. They burn cash. They experiment. Some fail. Others take years to become commercially successful.

The Migration Advisory Committee (MAC) has recommended abolishing the Innovator Founder Visa in its current form or substantially reforming it.

Imagine a venture capital fund abandoning startup investments because its portfolio wasn't profitable within the first few years.

Of course, the MAC raises legitimate concerns about business performance, low earnings and economic contribution. All of these concerns have genuine answers that were unfortunately overlooked.

I'm all in for reforms - redefine the criteria and fix the system where appropriate, especially in the post-AI era.

I believe the reforms should focus on the following areas.

Redefining innovation: AI has dramatically expanded human thinking and problem-solving capabilities. What constitutes genuine innovation in this new environment, and how should it be measured?

Founder capabilities: Assess relevant experience, commercial judgement, leadership and the ability to assemble and manage the right team, rather than disproportionately prioritising technical qualifications. 

Commercial prospects: Commercial and economic impact of the proposed businesses by sector. Applying the same criteria to all sector businesses is not practical. Some sectors could be risky, some could have a lot of room for growth and success. The evidence requirement in both cases could vary greatly.

Investment at risk: Consider the financial commitment and resources genuinely at risk in developing and commercialising the business.

Scalability and economic impact: Evaluate realistic growth potential, job creation, export opportunities and long-term economic contribution.

These criteria should form a transparent, evidence-based and measurable assessment framework, with clear scoring standards rather than inconsistent interpretations between assessors.

The assessment process itself also needs reform.

Applicants spend months developing business plans and MVPs, yet some receive generic rejections without an opportunity to defend their propositions. This is turning away high potential applicants to other routes. 

A mandatory interview before a final rejection would allow founders to explain their innovation, demonstrate differentiation and respond directly to assessors' concerns.

Having worked with hundreds of entrepreneurs, I believe the objective should be to identify people capable of building commercially successful, scalable businesses, not simply those with the most technically novel proposals.

Should we abolish the route because of initial stats, or reform how we identify and assess entrepreneurial potential?

I'd be interested to hear the views of founders, endorsing bodies and immigration professionals.

MATERNAL MORTALITY: THE LABORATORY’S ROLE IN SAVING LIVES BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER CHILDBIRTH.

When we discuss maternal mortality, attention often focuses on obstetric emergencies, antenatal care and access to skilled birth attendants. However, one critical aspect deserves more attention: the Medical Laboratory.

According to WHO estimates, Nigeria recorded a maternal mortality ratio of 993 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2023.

So, how does laboratory medicine contribute to preventing these deaths?

1. Early detection of anaemia: Full Blood Count (FBC) helps identify anaemia and allows timely intervention before childbirth.

2. Prevention of transfusion delays: Blood grouping, Rh typing, antibody screening and crossmatching support transfusion preparedness during obstetric haemorrhage, a major cause of maternal death.

3. Detection of pre-eclampsia complications: Platelet counts, renal function tests, liver function tests and urine protein assessment support clinical evaluation and monitoring.

4. Identification of infections: Urine culture, blood cultures and other microbiological investigations help identify infections and guide appropriate treatment, reducing the risk of maternal sepsis.

5. Antenatal screening: Investigations for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, blood group and Rh status help identify risks requiring early intervention.

However, performing these investigations is not enough.

We must also ensure:

* Accurate and reliable results.
* Timely processing and reporting.
* Effective communication of critical results.
* Availability of essential reagents and blood products.
* Functional blood banking and transfusion services.
* Strong collaboration among healthcare professionals.

A laboratory result delivered too late may lose its clinical value. Accuracy and timely reporting can make a significant difference in patient outcomes.

Maternal mortality prevention is a shared responsibility.

As Medical Laboratory Scientists, we may not always be at the bedside, but our work contributes to the decisions that save lives.

Because behind every sample is a patient, and sometimes, a life depending on what we find.

The recent outage that hit Microsoft's services for nearly a full day was remarkable for its scale and its duration, and it comes in a series: Revolut on 20 October, JPMorgan Chase's online banking on 16 November, Apple's services on 17 November. Every large platform has bad days, and the engineers who run them are very good at their work, while platform complexity reaches unprecedented scale. Some attribute these failures to under-investment in critical capacities redirected toward AI projects, others to a premature race to automation that triggers chain reactions. 

What is striking is that they hit basic functions, such as e-mail, of hyperscalers that preempt ever more floors of the enterprise application stack. A platform in that position has to keep its foundations impeccable and also absorb innovations that mostly arrive from outside, which invites a broader question: how we have built enterprise information systems for twenty years, and whether it suits the road they now have to travel.

For that, I would like to use an analogy that is dear to me: the tyre.

Solid rubber tyres came before the pneumatic ones, and they still serve where the speed is low and the ground predictable. Consolidating applications, platforms and identities under a single contract was a similar choice, and for a long time it was the right one. As the road becomes less predictable, its limit appears: ten applications that depend on the same identity service are not ten independent solutions, and on a bad day they fail as a group.

A modern tyre is a volume of air held by textile plies, steel belts and several rubber compounds, bonded together, with a tread that wears out and can be replaced while the casing stays. I wonder whether it offers a model for the information system: a flexible composite, whose durable core (identity, data, security rules) holds while the changeable layers (applications, models, agents) can be swapped quickly as the road changes. That asks for the right pressure, neither so loose that shadow IT takes over nor so tight that people work around the rules, and for decisions as fast as the life of what they decide: months of ROI studies suit something built to last ten years, not a tool that may be out of date in a few months.

A composite has its own risk, which sits at the interfaces between its layers. And I suspect that the larger cost of the solid tyre is what never reaches us, because an innovation often arrives once a suite has assimilated it.

Simplifying an architecture has long been read as a sign of maturity. On a road that keeps changing, at what point does it become a loss of grip?

I have shared more reflections on this subject in the article below, curious to get your thoughts!

A Digital Service Can Work Perfectly While the Institution Behind It Is in Trouble

One thing I find interesting about digital transformation is how easily we can confuse the quality of a service with the strength of the institution providing it.

A banking application can be easy to use.

Transactions can be processed quickly.

Customers can have a convenient experience.

But none of these things, on their own, tells us whether the institution has adequate financial controls, responsible governance or effective risk management.

The Ueno Bank situation in Paraguay is a reminder of this distinction.

On November 3, 2026, Paraguay’s Central Bank announced that it was placing Ueno into resolution after adjustments to its financial statements revealed a serious capital adequacy deficiency.

The regulator said the bank’s solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum.

That is a very different problem from whether its mobile application worked properly.

And I think this distinction matters beyond financial services.

When we use a digital platform, we interact with its interface. We rarely see the full institutional arrangements behind it.

We don’t necessarily see how decisions are made, how risks are assessed, how information is governed or how accountability is maintained.

Yet these are the things that ultimately support the service we experience.

This raises a question worth considering whenever an organisation introduces a new digital service:

Are we evaluating only what the technology can do, or are we also examining the institution and controls behind it?

Digital trust cannot rest entirely on a smooth user experience.

It also requires responsible governance, transparency, accountability and the ability to manage problems when they arise.

The interface may be what customers see.

But the institution behind it is what they ultimately depend on.

The Global Network of Director Institutes (GNDI) Global Conference 2026 has just wrapped up with an insightful panel discussion featuring Maria Pierdicchi, Chair of ecoDa, and Laurent DEGABRIEL, CEO of the French Institute of Directors (IFA).

🔎 The discussion brought together global perspectives on the challenges shaping board agendas today, with several important takeaways:

👉 Geopolitical and economic uncertainty: Persistent macroeconomic and microeconomic volatility makes long-term planning increasingly challenging. Boards must remain agile, anticipate different scenarios and adapt to change without losing sight of long-term objectives.
👉 AI as a fiduciary responsibility: AI should not be treated simply as another item on the board agenda, but as a strategic and fiduciary responsibility requiring informed oversight.
👉 The future of ESG: The priority should be to provide reliable and meaningful sustainability information without creating unnecessary complexity.
👉 From compliance to entrepreneurship: Boards need to develop a more entrepreneurial mindset, moving beyond a purely compliance-driven approach towards more active, forward-looking and timely decision-making.
New leadership models: Organisations need to develop leadership models and strengthen board competencies to respond to an increasingly complex and rapidly changing environment.

📢 One overarching message stood out: boards need to move from oversight to foresight – anticipating change, embracing innovation and keeping people at the centre of transformation.

Thank you to Maria and Laurent for sharing their perspectives, and to GNDI for bringing the global governance community together!

Great as always to catch up with clients, colleagues and contacts at the UK Finance Annual Dinner last night. We were the last table to leave, which I think says a lot about the relationships we have as a team and that we build with our clients. 

My key takeaways from the speeches were:

🔹 David Postings, CEO, UK Finance 

• Fraud and Big Tech: tech platforms should take more responsibility for tackling fraud. Banks currently bear a disproportionate share of the cost. 
• Agentic payments: liability should follow control. Banks should answer for their own systems, not for AI agents outside their control. (This goes beyond payments: firms deciding whether to allow third-party agents or build their own must weigh the liability and regulatory risks carefully.) 
• Capital: are UK banks holding too much once management buffers are counted? 
• Tech investment: other jurisdictions treat intangibles more favourably for capital purposes. That leaves UK banks choosing between investing in technology and supporting lending. 

🔹 Katharine Braddick, PRA 

• Transparency: the PRA wants to provide more clarity on supervisory priorities, the reasons for decisions and, where possible, how firms compare with peers. 
• Predictability: less discretion in Basel 3 implementation and the Strong and Simple regime from January. In return, the PRA expects firms to be transparent with supervisors. 
• Engagement: an open invitation to banks and insurers to say where the framework could be clearer or more effective. 
• Resilience: escalating non-financial risks are a growing priority, with a focus on basic cyber hygiene. Shared technology and third-party dependencies need collective solutions, building on CMORG's work. 
• New Systemic Resilience Council: a forum to coordinate industry and regulators, starting with frontier AI risks and recovery from severe cyber disruption. This could be a significant step for collective operational resilience.

🔹 Rt Hon Lucy Rigby KC MP, Economic Secretary to the Treasury 

A supportive message on the sector's contribution to the UK economy, plus: • Digital gilts: issuance targeted for Q1 2027. 
• Digital assets: the cryptoasset authorisation regime comes into force next year, and the UK moves into delivery. 
• FOS reform: the FCA sets policy and rules, and the FOS applies them. 
• Regulation: an ambition for proportionate and facilitative regulation.

Thank you to everyone who joined us, and to Angela Greenough, Ruth Jones and George Gledhill for helping to make the evening a success.

Amazon PPC gives you plenty of data.

Clicks, CPC, CTR, CVR, ACoS, placements, and search terms.

But more data doesn't always mean better decisions.

Sometimes, it creates more confusion.

Here's where advertisers go wrong:

→ Short-Term Reactions: Changing bids after one bad day without enough evidence.

→ Small Sample Sizes: Pausing a keyword after a few clicks with no orders.

→ Ignoring Context: Comparing performance without considering seasonality, competition, or promotions.

→ Metric Isolation: Optimizing ACoS without checking sales volume and contribution profit.

→ Data Overload: Tracking too many metrics without knowing which ones matter for the campaign's objective.

→ Attribution Delays: Making decisions before all advertising sales have been reported.

For example, a keyword gets 15 clicks and zero orders.

Does that mean it's unprofitable?

Not necessarily. Its historical CVR, CPC, and product economics matter.

My approach?

Start with the business objective, identify the relevant metrics, and evaluate performance over a meaningful period.

Then make changes based on patterns, not isolated numbers.

Good PPC optimization isn't about having more data. It's about knowing which data deserves your attention.

From a single crowded hotel in Texas to a global empire of nearly 9,500 properties—it all proves that great empires are built on resilience.

Understanding the balance sheet starts with one fundamental distinction: Assets vs. Liabilities.
​While both are essential to running and scaling a business, they play opposite roles in your financial health:
​🔹 Assets (What you own & control): Resources that generate future economic value—like cash, inventory, equipment, and intellectual property.
🔹 Liabilities (What you owe): Obligations that require future cash outflows—like accounts payable, loans, bonds, and accrued expenses.
​Together, they anchor the core accounting equation:
Assets = Liabilities + Equity
​Strong businesses don't just grow assets—they manage how those assets are funded between debt (liabilities) and ownership (equity).
​Which financial metric do you look at first when evaluating a company's balance sheet?

At our event with Robin Wall Kimmerer and Kate Raworth, Kate told us about the circus she stages at festivals and conferences. 

She is the ringmaster, and audience members play Mother Nature and Finance, the extractive, accumulating character with a briefcase that sucks up the returns of the world.

When someone steps up to play Greed, Kate brings in Robin’s Honourable Harvest, read slowly, as if Robin were in the room. Time and again, greed softens. “These words invite us back into relation", said Kate. 

 The honorable harvest is a set of principles for taking from the living world in a way that sustains it, described by Robin Wall Kimmerer in Braiding Sweetgrass. For example: 
🌿 Take only what you need. Never take more than half, so the rest can keep growing and feeding others.

 🍒 Give thanks and give back. Receive what’s offered as a gift, and answer it with gratitude and reciprocity.

Kimmerer, a citizen of the Potawatomi Nation, draws on Indigenous teachings, and many Indigenous cultures hold their own traditions of respectful, reciprocal relationship with the land. The Honourable Harvest is one expression of a much wider body of knowledge.

It was beautiful to witness Robin's warm smile as Kate introduced her circus, which makes complex issues tangible and fun!

Entrepreneurs are shaping a new chapter in Iraq’s history by turning the country's rich heritage into business opportunities, as I saw firsthand during a recent visit to Baghdad.

I met Zainab Raad Jassim, founder of Shaar Banat, which means "cotton candy" in Arabic. Her business reimagines a popular street food into customizable desserts, including a cotton candy cake featuring the International Trade Centre logo.
   
It’s a reminder that finding business success comes from understanding the customer, adding value and finding creative ways to stand out in an increasingly global marketplace.
  
Zainab's journey also shows what’s possible when entrepreneurs have the right support. Through one of our projects, she received a business grant and business development services through our partner, Norwegian Refugee Council.

Stories like hers resonated in a week that saw nearly €15.3 million in potential business deals generated at the Iraq National Trade and Investment Forum – where nearly half of participating companies were women-owned – and in discussions with the Prime Minister, as well as the Minister of Trade Dr. Mustafa Nazar and Minister of Foreign Affairs Fuad Hussein. Our conversations reflected a shared understanding that Iraq’s long-term prosperity lies in economic diversification, private sector growth and deeper integration into regional and global markets.
   
That means focusing on three priorities.
  
First, advancing trade and investment reforms that create the predictable business environment investors seek. Iraq’s World Trade Organization accession process and the development of a new National Trade and Investment Strategy are important steps in that direction.
  
Second, investing in the private sector. Small businesses account for 90% of companies and employ two-thirds of the workforce. Supporting their growth through skills, market access, financing and stronger value chains is key.
  
Third, building partnerships that connect policy ambitions to business opportunities. Much of our work, led by the government and implemented by our in-country team, is made possible through our strong partnership with the EU.

Economic transformation ultimately comes down to people: entrepreneurs who see opportunity where others see obstacles, women building businesses, youth creating jobs, small businesses turning local products, skills and traditions into incomes, growth and resilience.

Funny how experience suddenly becomes fashionable again.

in july 2018, borisov and karadzhov started Payhawk with a simple ambition, bring corporate cards, expenses and accounting into one platform. 

they began as a two-person engineering team, selling the idea to businesses before they even had a working product.

what followed was a steady growth, a €3 million seed round, a $20 million Series A led by QED Investors, a $112 million Series B led by Greenoaks, and a $100 million extension led by Lightspeed that valued Payhawk at a billion $ back in 2022.

now comes the next chapter.

Payhawk has raised $280 million in Series C, led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, taking its total funding to $515 million and its valuation to $2 billion.

existing investors QED Investors, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures participated, alongside new investors including Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus. 

Entrepreneurs Tomas Okmanas and Dídac Lee also joined the round.

interesting part isn't just the valuation.

Payhawk is moving beyond corporate cards and expense management towards what it calls a "Finance Operating System for the ai era'.

its ambition is to combine ai agents that handle expense reconciliation, procurement, travel and financial reporting with payments infrastructure and enterprise controls that determine how money can move and when human approval is needed.

and it matters, so much because most finance software helps teams record and monitor transactions. 

Payhawk goes a step ahead and aims its agents to actually execute the work around those transactions.

and it's a much bigger market to go after than expense management alone.

from two engineers selling an idea with wireframes in Sofia to a $2 billion fintech backed by one of the biggest investment bankers in the globe, Goldman Sachs.

the founders are no longer just building a better way to manage company spending.
they want to automate the finance function itself.

Europe’s startup story is increasingly about scale, and the next stage of growth may depend on how effectively its companies connect with capital and customers beyond the continent. 

That opportunity will be in focus at Expand North Star 2026, taking place in Dubai from 8–10 December.

The event will bring delegations from Austria, France, Germany, Italy and Serbia, alongside exhibitors from Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Finland, the Netherlands and the UK. Their presence comes as Dealroom estimates the combined value of Europe’s VC-backed companies at $4.4 trillion, while startups raised $67.2 billion in venture capital during the first nine months of 2026, already above the full-year 2025 total.

AI is a major part of that momentum. European AI startups attracted $38.3 billion in the same period, surpassing the previous annual record of $21.8 billion set in 2025. The figures point to an ecosystem with substantial capital and technical depth, but international expansion remains a key route to turning that strength into broader commercial reach.

Italy is bringing 30 startups and SMEs through the Italian Trade Agency, spanning AI, cybersecurity, healthtech, life sciences, industrial technology, clean tech and fintech. 

Companies including Tinental, Realynx, AI4IV,smartFAB and ATACOD will present technologies ranging from AI-enabled industrial systems to cybersecurity and robotics. 

Valerio Soldani, Trade Commissioner to the UAE and Oman, said the agency aims to help participating companies secure growth capital, develop commercial projects and build partnerships in the region.

Serbia’s delegation, led by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Serbia (PKS), highlights another dimension of the opportunity. Startup Genome reports that half of Serbian startups are integrating AI or machine learning, around two-thirds plan international expansion, and 76.2% are developing IP-rich products for global markets. 

PKS President Marko Čadez sees scope for two-way cooperation, with Serbian companies entering Gulf markets and UAE investors exploring opportunities in Serbia and Southeast Europe.

That ambition will also be supported by the launch of GITEX AI Belgrade on 25–27 May 2027, extending the GITEX network into Southeast Europe. At Expand North Star, European founders will meet more than 1,000 investors from 60 countries, managing a combined $2 trillion in assets. The bigger question is whether these connections can translate into sustained investment, market access and commercial partnerships across regions.

Whale Theory in Business Strategy | Are We Focusing on the Right Customers?

Not every customer contributes equally to business growth.

The Whale Theory highlights an interesting business principle: a relatively small number of high-value customers can drive a significant proportion of an organisation's revenue and long-term growth. But the real strategy isn't just about identifying these customers. It's about understanding their business priorities, building trust, delivering exceptional value and nurturing relationships that evolve into long-term strategic partnerships.

A few lessons worth remembering:
- Focus on value, not just volume.
- Build relationships beyond individual transactions.
- Understand customer challenges before proposing solutions.
- Look for opportunities to grow together.
- Prioritise long-term partnerships over short-term wins.

The bigger question isn't how many customers we serve, but how much meaningful value we create for them.
Because sustainable growth comes from building partnerships, not just expanding customer lists.

What's your perspective? Do you believe businesses should prioritise high-value accounts or focus equally on every customer?

Dreaming Won't Build Your Startup. Taking the First Step Will

Today, I attended an event and came back with a valuable lesson, especially for every startup founder and aspiring entrepreneur.

I learned that three qualities are extremely important in life and business:

ABC of Success:

🔹 A – Availability: Be available when opportunities come your way. Show up, participate, and be present.

🔹 B – Behaviour: Your attitude, communication, and how you treat people define your personality and build long-term relationships.

🔹 C – Capability: Having the skills, knowledge, and ability to turn opportunities into results.

There was another beautiful story shared at the event.

A person wanted to start a business and prayed to God every day, asking for a lottery ticket to win so he could get money to start his business.

He kept praying day and night.

One day, God appeared and said:

"I really want to help you win the lottery, but at least buy a lottery ticket first!"


That story made me think.

Everyone wants to become an entrepreneur. Everyone wants funding, investors, opportunities, and success. But how many are actually willing to take the first step?

- You want to start a startup, but have you started working on your idea?
- You want investment, but have you prepared your business model?
- You want opportunities, but are you networking?
- You want success, but are you taking action?

Stop waiting for the perfect opportunity. Start with whatever you have.

Because even God needs you to take the first step! 😊

2,500 hours of executive coaching.
And the biggest obstacle to success is not what I expected.
It's not intelligence.
It's not experience.
It's not a lack of ambition.
It's the invisible prison of our own beliefs.
After 2,500 hours of coaching executives, entrepreneurs and business leaders, five lessons stand out:
1. The need to be right can prevent us from growing.
2. The fear of disappointing others can lead us to disappoint ourselves.
3. What made us successful yesterday can become our biggest limitation tomorrow.
4. The most difficult conversations are often the ones we need to have with ourselves.
5. Real leadership begins when we no longer need to prove that we are leaders.
We spend years learning how to manage businesses, build strategies, negotiate deals and lead teams.

Yet the most challenging person we will ever have to lead is ourselves.

Life is not a video game.

But we all have invisible barriers to break, challenges to overcome and new levels to unlock.
And sometimes, reaching the next level requires unlearning rather than learning.

The ultimate leadership challenge is not changing others. It's changing yourself.

Yesterday I wrote as a founder. Today I changed chairs.
Investors ask founders four questions:
Do you have a license? Are you on Apple and Google? Users? Three months of revenue?
I used to call them absurd. Sitting in the investor's chair, I see I was half wrong. They are a flashlight to tell a real business from a beautiful story.
So here are my honest answers:
— License to accept payments: not yet. That is what the money is for.
— App Store and Google Play: yes, already there.
— Users: almost none, on purpose — no mass invitations before a license.
— Revenue: practically zero. But the reserve is open for anyone to check.
Two people sit at that table, and both are afraid. Deals fail not because of fear, but when each side hides it behind a role.

🤖 The use of artificial intelligence by insurance companies and intermediaries may involve different supervisory authorities, depending on the functions performed by the system.

🏛️ Legislative Decree 179/2026 defines the supervisory powers and the national framework of sanctions for the implementation of the AI Act.

⚖️ IVASS is responsible for supervising high-risk systems directly linked to insurance, reinsurance and distribution activities. These include, in particular, systems used for risk assessment and pricing for individuals in life and health insurance. For other systems, such as conversational assistants and generative tools for text and communications that do not fall within the high-risk category, supervision is the responsibility of the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN), in collaboration with IVASS.

📃 The decree also addresses customer protection: the Insurance Ombudsman gains jurisdiction over appeals concerning breaches of the AI Act committed by participating undertakings and intermediaries, within the limits of the supervisory powers assigned to IVASS and the activities already falling within the Ombudsman’s remit. The classification of individual systems is therefore of key importance, as it determines the relevant authorities, obligations and protective measures. Deadlines also require attention: the obligations for high-risk systems listed in Annex III, including those relating to life and health insurance pricing, will apply from 2 December 2027, without this entailing a general postponement of the obligations for other uses of AI.

#Floreani #Divincenzo #IVASS #AI

It was his personality.

His infectious smile, his humour, his warmth and the way he appeared to genuinely enjoy engaging with people.

SEVEN YEARS OF FLY CONNECT. THE VISION WAS NEVER JUST TO BUILD A TRAVEL COMPANY.

Seven years ago, I founded Fly Connect on a conviction that has continued to shape my understanding of business and global opportunity.Geography should not determine the limits of human potential.

I envisioned an institution that would transcend borders, connect people to global possibilities and position Africa as an active participant in the exchange of talent, knowledge, capital and opportunity. But I understood something early: a vision, no matter how ambitious, is only as powerful as the structures built to sustain it.

Over the last seven years, I've had the privilege of translating that vision into an operating business, building teams, expanding our presence, establishing international relationships and creating pathways for people to pursue opportunities beyond their immediate environments.

It has been a journey of strategy, calculated risks, difficult decisions and continuous reinvention.

And perhaps the greatest lesson has been this:
Entrepreneurship is not merely the art of creating something that works. It is the discipline of building something that can evolve, multiply value and remain relevant beyond its founder.

I've learned to think beyond transactions, beyond immediate revenue and beyond the excitement of expansion. Because a truly sustainable enterprise must be built on more than ambition. It requires institutional competence, financial discipline, exceptional people, systems that scale and leadership capable of anticipating change.

Today, as Fly Connect marks its seventh anniversary, I celebrate much more than the passage of time.

I celebrate an idea that became an enterprise.
A vision that created opportunities.
The people who gave their talent to its development.
The clients who entrusted us with important chapters of their lives.
And the partners who recognised the possibilities we were working to create.
To everyone who has contributed to this journey, I remain deeply grateful.

But my greatest excitement is not about what we've accomplished. It's about what we're positioning ourselves to become.

The future of global mobility is being redefined by technology, changing economies, international partnerships and evolving human aspirations. And I intend for Fly Connect to remain an active participant in that transformation, not simply a spectator.

Our next chapter is about institutional strength, innovation, strategic expansion and building an enterprise whose relevance extends across markets and generations.

Seven years ago, I founded a company.
Today, I'm more intentional about building an institution.
Connecting Africa to the World. Connecting the World to Africa.

Happy 7th Anniversary to Fly Connect.
The vision was never limited to the present. And neither is our future.

“Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.” — Brené Brown

This is one of those leadership lessons that sounds simple but isn’t always easy to put into practice.

Especially if you’re someone who genuinely cares about people.

How many times have we hesitated to have a difficult conversation because we didn’t want to hurt someone’s feelings? Or softened our feedback so much that the person walked away without really understanding what needed to change?

In my years as a clinician, coach, and business owner, I’ve come to appreciate how important it is to balance empathy with accountability.

Sometimes, in our efforts to protect someone’s feelings, we unintentionally rob them of an opportunity to grow.

Being direct doesn’t mean being unkind. We can have honest conversations with compassion, communicate expectations with respect, and hold people accountable while still being their biggest cheerleader.

It’s something I continue to work on.

Maybe one of the kindest things we can do for someone is care enough about their success to have the conversation we’d rather avoid.

#Leadership #Empathy #Accountability #Communication

The Future of Artificial Intelligence: Agentic AI Explained in Simple Terms


Artificial Intelligence has become part of everyday work. Professionals use it to write emails, summarize reports, generate ideas, analyze data, and answer questions within seconds. These tools have helped businesses become faster and more efficient, but a new generation of AI is taking productivity even further.

AI is becoming unstoppable. Within minutes, the AI researches customer trends, drafts marketing content, creates a project timeline, schedules follow-up reminders, prepares reports, and recommends the next steps. Rather than waiting for instructions after every task, it works toward completing the entire goal.

Truth be told, that’s not a simple AI itself, but the power of Agentic AI.

Agentic AI is an advanced form of Artificial Intelligence designed to accomplish objectives instead of responding to one prompt at a time. Unlike traditional AI that performs individual tasks based on direct user instructions, Agentic AI generates text, answers questions, creates images, or analyzes information only after receiving a specific prompt.

After receiving a prompt, Agentic AI can analyze the situation, develop a plan, perform multiple connected tasks, evaluate outcomes, adjust its actions when necessary, and continue working until the objective is completed. It combines reasoning, planning, memory, workflow automation, and integration with business applications to execute processes more intelligently.

🎓 Raphael Bednarsky and I just celebrated the successful defense of our very first co-supervised Master’s thesis student!

🎉 Huge congratulations to 𝐀𝐧𝐝𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬 𝐇𝐨𝐟𝐞𝐫 on defending his Master’s thesis, "𝐴𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑐 𝑆𝑐𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑐 𝐷𝑎𝑡𝑎 𝐴𝑛𝑎𝑙𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑠 𝑤𝑖𝑡ℎ 𝑆𝑛𝑎𝑘𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑘𝑒," at TU Wien!

⏱️ What makes this achievement even more impressive is the execution: Andreas kicked off the project with us in March and successfully defended by November: completing a full design, implementation, and benchmarking study in record time, all while juggling ongoing coursework and a software developer job.

🧭 Co-supervising him on a daily basis in Christoph Bock’𝐬 lab at CeMM and the Institute of Artificial Intelligence at Medical University of Vienna has been a genuinely rewarding experience.

🧬 Together, we tackled a core challenge in AI-assisted science: how to make AI-driven bioinformatics reproducible, inspectable, and affordable rather than relying on opaque, ad-hoc generated, unvalidated scripts.

🔬 Here is what Andreas built and demonstrated using #MrBiomics [https://lnkd.in/drMYTPRz], our framework of composable Snakemake workflows:

🧩 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: Instead of letting AI agents code analyses from scratch, we equipped them with expert-curated procedural context to compose, and execute validated MrBiomics #Snakemake modules end-to-end.

⚙️ 𝐑𝐢𝐠𝐨𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠: Andreas built a deterministic test harness and ran >𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 across models, harnesses, and context ablations on a real-world multi-step bioinformatics task.

📈 𝐒𝐎𝐓𝐀 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐜𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐛𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐭: Combining an open-source harness, a resource-efficient model, and our context matched frontier coding agent performance while cutting costs by 69%, thereby making large-scale agentic scientific analysis feasible.

🤝 This project was also a fantastic cross-institutional collaboration with Jürgen Cito’s lab and Jakob Hoffmann at Technische Universität Wien. As a #TUWien alumnus, it felt especially great to be back at my alma mater, bridging software engineering and biomedical data science across Vienna’s research institutions.

🚀 Stay tuned! We are currently writing up these results as part of the upcoming 𝐌𝐫𝐁𝐢𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐜𝐬 preprint, there is much more to share soon on how composable workflows can power reliable AI-assisted discovery.

👏 Once again, congratulations Andreas: we couldn't have asked for a better first Master's student, and we're excited to see what you build next!

⁉️ LEGO DIDN'T NEED MORE IDEAS. IT NEEDED FEWER.
In 2004, LEGO was fighting for survival.
The Danish company had expanded into new products, businesses, and experiences.
Innovation was everywhere.
But complexity was growing faster than the organization could manage.
The number of different LEGO elements had exploded from around 6,000 to over 14,000 in just seven years.
👉 More products. More components. More operational complexity.
And less profitability.
Then came a radical shift under CEO Jørgen Vig Knudstorp.
Instead of adding more initiatives, LEGO refocused on its core business, simplified its product portfolio, and dramatically reduced complexity.
By 2005, the company was profitable again.
💡 The paradox? Sometimes the most effective growth strategy starts with doing less.
This is a lesson for every leadership team.
Strategy is not simply deciding what to pursue.
🎯 It is having the discipline to decide what to stop.
Food for thought:
What could your organization achieve if it eliminated 20% of its current initiatives and redirected that energy toward its most important priorities?
At Tonus Consulting, through PRAKSIS, I help leaders turn strategic priorities into focused, disciplined execution.
Do the right things. Do them better.
www.tonusconsulting.com

I recently took my wife's car to the workshop for a repair, and the experience reminded me of a common challenge in engineering leadership.

The mechanic was clearly skilled at his trade, yet he immediately began explaining the problem through diagnostic fault codes, sensor readings, and system detailed functionality.

Standing at the counter, my mind was trying to translate that technical detail into something I could explain to my wife, which came down to three simple questions:

- What is the immediate safety and operational risk?
- What are my realistic options?
- And what is the true cost of each option compared to doing nothing?

That small moment at the workshop mirrors what happens every day in complex asset management and engineering.

When you spend your week deep inside technical systems, it is natural to think and speak in tolerances, failure modes, and specifications. Yet when you step into a broader strategic room with people from operations, finance, or executive leadership, they are listening for something different. They want to know what an engineering issue means for service reliability, safety, and long term value.

Years ago, I remember reading Herbert Simon's work on bounded rationality and his famous essay "Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World", where he observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.

Reflecting on his work now, the practical lesson for engineers is clear. When decision makers are already stretched across competing priorities, giving them more raw technical data does not improve their decision.

Our role is to filter the noise and structure the information around what truly matters.

To bridge that gap between technical depth and strategic clarity, I now frame major engineering discussions around the same three questions: what happens if we do nothing, what are the realistic options on the table, and what is the trade off.

Simplifying must not hide uncertainty. Decision makers still need to know what is known, what is inferred, and what is not yet verified.

Translating physics into real world business impact does not lower our engineering standards. It respects the audience enough to make the reasoning behind a decision transparent, turning technical expertise into shared confidence.

#EngineeringLeadership #AssetManagement #StrategicCommunication

📢 New Article in #IRAS: The sociotechnical design of smart city projects: A configurational approach for service innovation 📢

Authors: Emanuele Gabriel Margherita, Giovanni Esposito, Stefania Denise Escobar, PhD, and Nathalie Crutzen

This study advances the smart city literature by developing a sociotechnical design perspective on how projects are associated with intended service innovation outcomes. Prior research has examined social aspects—such as inter-organizational arrangements and human resource capabilities—and technological solutions, including digital technologies and artificial intelligence, largely in isolation, with limited attention to how their alignment shapes intended service innovation outcomes. Using an original dataset of 88 smart city projects developed by Belgian municipalities, we apply fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis to identify distinct sociotechnical configurations. The results reveal three pathways: (a) artificial intelligence-driven innovation via public–private partnerships, relying on external expertise; (b) co-development of digital technologies through public–private partnerships and human resource training, reflecting a capability-building logic; and (c) implementation of digital technologies through public tendering and training, representing an internally conceived but externally executed approach.

MICE Matters (Student Edition): Why I got fired from my job…

I got fired. Not a particularly pleasant experience. But looking back, a valuable lesson in life.

I was working for a large US-owned agency in the UK.

Three reasons why I lost my job.

* Revenues were falling.
* My role wasn’t directly generating revenue. 
* Management valued the contribution of others more than mine.

Harsh? Perhaps. But business isn’t a charity.

There are three lessons here for anyone starting out in our industry.

First. Are you adding value, or are you adding cost?

It’s a question you should ask yourself regularly. Not once a year at your appraisal. Every day.

If your employer cannot see the value you bring, don’t be surprised when someone questions the cost of employing you.

Second. Economic cycles are inevitable.

Businesses grow. Businesses contract. Good people can still lose their jobs.

Job security is never guaranteed, however impressive the company name above the door.

Third. Size matters.

I would argue that working in a smaller business can give you greater influence over your own destiny.

You are more likely to be seen as a person, rather than a number on a spreadsheet or a name on an organisation chart.

But there’s something more important.

ATTITUDE.

Particularly early in your career, I believe that attitude matters more than ability.

You can teach someone how to manage a rooming list. It’s considerably harder to teach them to give a damn.

Three simple ways to demonstrate the right attitude:

Take ownership. Don’t just identify problems. Help solve them.

Be useful. Look for what needs doing, not simply what’s in your job description.

Be someone others want alongside them. Particularly when things get difficult.

Now, back to my dismissal.

There was a fourth reason I lost my job.

My attitude stank.

I felt I had been passed over for a promotion, and had been negative about the organisation with colleagues as a result, and after 5 years a 200 mile daily commute had finally ground me down. 

Frankly I was a problem, two senior managers did their best to turn me around but the financial situation was inevitably going to force matters.

I could however see the writing on the wall months in advance. It wasn’t difficult to spot.

I left on a Friday, went on holiday for a week and started a new job at a small event agency the following Monday much closer to home.

Financially, I’d dodged a bullet.

Emotionally, it was still traumatic. Being told you’re no longer wanted is a deeply unpleasant experience.

But I learned something that has stayed with me throughout the decades that followed.

Your ability might get you hired. Your attitude will have a considerable influence on whether you stay, progress or find yourself surplus to requirements.

And never forget, someone is paying for you to be there.

Make sure you’re worth it.

I am utterly grateful to have been part of the Second Cohort of the BCX Women in Leadership Programme.
The past 6 months have been transformative, challenging and incredibly enriching. The programme's commitment to developing and empowering women to take up leadership roles across the business and in every space they occupy has been a truly valuable experience.

As this chapter comes to an end, one thing is certain: the learning does not end here. The real journey lies in applying the lessons, insights and reflections gained along the way. This is not an ending, but the beginning of a new chapter.

One lesson I will carry with me is that impact can be gradual, but it still contributes to the bigger picture and the achievement of strategic goals. Never underestimate the value of the difference you make, even when the results are not immediately visible.

One of the most thought-provoking reflections shared during our graduation was that as women ascend the corporate hierarchy, motivation and ambition may grow, but empathy can decline.
May we never allow our pursuit of success to disconnect us from our humanity. As we rise as woman, may we continue to lead with kindness, remember our people and create spaces where others can thrive 💖.

A heartfelt thank you to the Learning and Development team and Experttech for putting together such an impactful programme, and for the invaluable coaching sessions with my amazing coach Anele Chonco, (MPhil Management Coaching). The insights, guidance and conversations have contributed immensely to this journey.
To my fellow cohort members, thank you for the shared experiences and lessons.

Here's to leading with purpose, courage, empathy and kindness. ❤️
#BCXWomenInLeadership #LeadershipJourney #WomenEmpowerment #LeadingWithEmpathy #ContinuousLearning. #TransformativeLeaderhsip.

My key takeaway from the Ghana Banking Conference was that the future of banking will be shaped by the intersection of trust, technology and transformation.

AI, digital assets and other emerging technologies present significant opportunities for banks, but technology alone will not create sustainable competitive advantage.

Banks must combine innovation with strong ethics, governance, regulatory compliance and, importantly, a deep understanding of changing customer needs.

For me, the practical lesson is that we need to use technology not simply to digitise existing processes, but to rethink how we create value for customers, improve efficiency and develop more integrated solutions across customer value chains.

Highly commended! We’re delighted that our Cash Lab was highly commended for the Innovation Award at the 2026 Smart Thinking Awards, placing in the top four.

Run by the Policy Institute and School for Government at King's College London, the Cash Lab conducts randomised controlled trials to test whether unconditional cash transfers can tackle poverty and improve people’s lives.

Our first trial found that a one-off, no-strings-attached payment of £2,000 to young care leavers improved their likelihood of ending up in stable housing, with other positive impacts on their health and wellbeing. We look forward to sharing findings from upcoming trials in 2027.

Thank you to Smart Thinking, the judges and Lloyds Banking Group, and to our partners and funders. Most of all, thank you to everyone who has taken part in the trials.

Congratulations to the Cash Lab team – Michael Sanders, Hannah Piggott, Susannah Hume, Dimitris Vallis, Vanessa H., Julia Ellingwood, Paolo Morini and Connie Woollen – and to all our fellow finalists!

The biggest breakthrough in my trading wasn't finding better strategies.

It was combining them.

Most traders evaluate strategies individually.

I became more interested in portfolios.

Different holding periods. Different market regimes. Different sources of return.

The objective was simple.

Reduce dependence on any single strategy. Reduce drawdowns. Improve consistency.

No strategy works all the time.

But a portfolio of genuinely different strategies can be surprisingly resilient.

That's one reason I believe portfolio construction is often more important than strategy selection.

The edge is not always in the strategy.

Sometimes it's in how the strategies work together.

🚀 Decoding Entrepreneurship | Episode 5: Startup Storytelling, Pitch Deck & Fundraising

A great startup idea is only the beginning. The real challenge is communicating that idea, telling its story, and convincing others to believe in your vision.

Continuing my journey through the Entrepreneurship Development Program (EDP) – Phase 7 at JECRC University, Episode 5 focused on Startup Storytelling, Pitch Deck & Fundraising.

It was a valuable and interactive session with Mayank B Nagori, Co-Founder of Gud Gum | The Better Chewing Gum, who shared practical insights from his entrepreneurial journey and his experience on Shark Tank India.

🔑 Key Learnings from the Session:

1️⃣ Storytelling Matters – A startup is not just about a product; its problem, purpose and journey make the story powerful.

2️⃣ Pitch with Clarity – Clearly communicate the problem, solution, target market and business opportunity.

3️⃣ Know Your Numbers – Passion attracts attention, but strong business fundamentals build credibility.

4️⃣ Learn from Feedback – Every question, rejection and feedback is an opportunity to improve.

5️⃣ Fundraising is More Than Money – Investors look at the founder, market potential, traction, vision and execution ability.

💡 What I Learned:

- Ideas Need Execution: An idea creates possibilities, but action turns it into reality.
- Storytelling Creates Connection: A strong story makes people understand and remember your idea.
- Numbers Tell the Business Story: Understanding your numbers helps you make better decisions and pitch confidently.
- Confidence Comes from Preparation: Preparation helps you handle questions and present your vision effectively.

⭐ One of my key takeaways:

"Your idea may get you started, but your ability to communicate that idea can take it further."

Hearing about Mayank B Nagori 's entrepreneurial journey and his Shark Tank India experience made the startup journey feel much more practical and relatable.

🚀 Investors Don't just Invest in Ideas. They Invest in Businesses That Are Ready to Grow. Is Your Startup Investor-Ready?

Having an innovative idea is important, but securing investment requires much more than an impressive business concept.
Before approaching investors, startup founders must ensure that their business is professionally prepared, financially transparent and strategically positioned.

Here are 5 critical areas every startup should prepare before approaching investors:
1. Financial Readiness
Maintain properly structured financial statements, revenue details, expense records, cash-flow projections and realistic financial forecasts.

2. A Strong Pitch Deck
Your presentation should clearly communicate the business problem, proposed solution, market opportunity, business model, competitive positioning and growth strategy.

3. Clear Shareholding Structure
Maintain updated shareholding details, capitalization tables, investment history and relevant shareholder agreements.

4. Legal & Compliance Readiness
Ensure that incorporation documents, statutory records, applicable tax filings, intellectual property records and material business agreements are properly maintained.

5. Clarity on Fund Utilisation
Investors want to understand how the proposed investment will be deployed, what milestones it will achieve and how it will contribute to business growth.
A common mistake founders make is approaching investors before preparing these fundamentals.
A well-prepared startup can present its business more confidently, respond effectively during due diligence and demonstrate its readiness for investment discussions.

→ Booking Concerns: Bookings continue across the scheduled network despite the operational shortfall.
→ Fundraising Initiative: The airline is reportedly looking to raise ₹5,500 crore to strengthen its financial position and support operations.
📌 The business lesson:
A company can have strong demand, brand recognition and market opportunity, but without operational execution and adequate working capital, growth becomes difficult to sustain.
For businesses and startups alike, three fundamentals remain critical:
• Operational efficiency
• Financial discipline
• Timely capital allocation
Growth is not just about demand. It is about having the capacity, capital and execution to deliver on that demand.

Una narrazione visiva capace di trasformare anche la più ordinaria delle banalità in un momento di apparente illuminazione collettiva.
Prendiamo un concetto semplice: «Il lavoro di squadra è importante».
Da solo, rischia di passare inosservato.
Ma se lo accompagniamo con cinque professionisti sorridenti, di etnie accuratamente distribuite, che si stringono la mano attorno a un tavolo olografico sospeso su una metropoli futuristica, ecco che tutto cambia.
Non stiamo più dicendo una banalità.
Stiamo generando valore.
E se una delle mani ha sei dita? Ancora meglio: significa che stiamo superando i limiti del pensiero convenzionale.
Ho quindi deciso di intraprendere anch'io questo percorso di evoluzione comunicativa.
D'ora in poi, ogni mia riflessione potrà contare su un ecosistema visuale coerente, caratterizzato da cervelli fluorescenti, circuiti blu, robot sorridenti e manager che osservano orizzonti digitali con l'espressione di chi ha appena scoperto l'acqua calda, ma in cloud.
Perché l'importante non è che l'immagine aggiunga qualcosa al contenuto.
L'importante è che sembri importantissima.
E soprattutto che tutti capiscano immediatamente che è stata generata in circa undici secondi, senza che questo intacchi minimamente la nostra percezione di autenticità.
Qualcuno potrebbe obiettare che stiamo progressivamente sostituendo l'originalità con una produzione industriale di suggestioni tutte uguali.
Io preferisco parlare di scalabilità dell'ispirazione.
Un cambio di paradigma.
Una nuova frontiera del personal branding.
In fondo, se tutti pubblicano lo stesso uomo in giacca che fissa lo stesso futuro luminoso, forse è perché quel futuro è davvero condiviso.
E io non voglio restare indietro.
Per questo ho scelto di fare il passo decisivo: smettere di affidare le mie idee alle sole parole e iniziare a circondarle della quantità di pixel sintetici che meritano.
Il contenuto passa.
Il robot con il pollice extra resta.
E voi? Avete già abbracciato il potere trasformativo delle immagini che non servono assolutamente a niente?

💭 When Code Can Create Almost Anything, What Remains Valuable?

For most of my career, I used code to build business applications.

C#, SQL Server, databases, workflows and enterprise systems.

Code was something I associated with solving technical and business problems.

But recently, something has changed in how I see it.

I've been experimenting with AI-generated illustrations, pixel art, motion graphics and a virtual aquarium where goldfish swim through a digitally created environment.

And I started wondering.

If code can create software, paintings, animations, music and entire virtual worlds, where does engineering end and creativity begin?

Of course, creative coding existed long before AI.

Artists, musicians and animators have used programming for decades.

But AI is making these possibilities accessible to people who never formally studied those disciplines.

Including someone like me.

At 45, I'm discovering creative possibilities I never seriously imagined exploring as a traditional software engineer.

It's exciting.

But it also raises uncomfortable questions.

If anyone can generate beautiful illustrations, what happens to professional illustrators?

If software can compose music, what happens to musicians?

If AI can generate code, what happens to software engineers?

I don't believe these questions have simple answers.

And I don't think producing something automatically means understanding the craft behind it.

A generated image isn't necessarily meaningful art.

A working animation isn't necessarily good storytelling.

Code that runs isn't necessarily good engineering.

The tools may become more powerful, but we still need to develop our ability to recognise quality, understand context and make thoughtful decisions.

Perhaps we're entering a period when producing something becomes increasingly easy, while deciding what deserves to be produced becomes more important.

That thought has stayed with me.

Because my journey with AI isn't just teaching me new tools.

It's challenging how I understand creativity, professional expertise and the value of human effort.

I'm still experimenting. Many of my results are imperfect.

But I'm starting to appreciate something.

Technology can expand what we're capable of creating.

It doesn't automatically tell us what is worth creating.

And perhaps that's where human imagination, experience and judgment continue to matter.

Engineers bring strong analytical rigor, structured problem-solving, and systems thinking into consulting. To move from technical execution to business strategy in 2026, focus on framing engineering work around cost, risk, revenue, and organizational impact.

1. Pick the Right Entry Niche

Start where your technical background gives you immediate credibility:
• AI & Implementation Consulting: Deploy and operationalize AI systems in production, manage human-AI workflows, and audit AI outputs.
• Cloud, SaaS & Security Advisory: Lead cloud migrations, multi-cloud modernization, enterprise software rollouts, and cybersecurity/compliance programs.
• Operations & Digital Transformation: Optimize supply chains, manufacturing, and business processes using data and systems thinking.
• Strategy & Generalist Consulting: Move into broader business strategy at firms like McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Deloitte, or PwC—often via campus hiring, an MBA, or experienced-hire routes.

2. Build Business Fluency

• Translate tech to ROI: Frame recommendations around cost savings, speed to value, risk mitigation, and stakeholder buy-in rather than technical elegance alone.
• Gain cross-functional exposure: Take on product, pricing, analytics, or transformation initiatives in your current role, or build business/finance fundamentals through coursework or an MBA.

3. Plan Your Timeline & Networking

• Set a realistic runway: Most users on Quora agree that career transition timelines typically span 6–12 months for smaller or internal consulting roles and 12–24 months for top-tier strategy consulting or MBA-led pivots.
• Network for referrals: Connect with engineers-turned-consultants, request informational chats, and target referrals rather than relying solely on cold applications.

4. Ace Consulting Interviews

• Case & structured problem-solving: Practice breaking ambiguous business problems into clear hypotheses, running quick math, and delivering concise recommendations.
• Behavioral & impact stories: Highlight leadership, stakeholder management, and measurable business outcomes from your engineering projects.

19 November 2026 | Shenzhen, China

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo has expressed interest in bringing technological advances observed at China’s Nanshan People’s Hospital in Shenzhen to Mexico’s public healthcare system.

Following a nearly two-hour visit on 18 November, Sheinbaum described the hospital as “very impressive”, highlighting its use of artificial intelligence to support disease identification, clinical diagnosis and treatment, alongside advanced medical equipment.

She was particularly struck by the hospital's automated operations: robots transport medicines and clinical samples between departments, while advanced equipment supports laboratory testing and patient care.

Speaking to reporters outside the hospital, Sheinbaum said her government had discussed establishing closer cooperation with China's ambassador to Mexico and the hospital's medical team to bring these scientific advances to Mexico.

The potential beneficiaries include Mexico's major public healthcare institutions: IMSS, IMSS-Bienestar and ISSSTE.

The President also noted that the Chinese and Mexican systems share a three-tier structure of primary, secondary and tertiary care, creating opportunities to exchange experience and practices.

No specific technology procurement, implementation timetable or funding agreement has yet been announced. The immediate step is to explore cooperation and identify advances that could be adapted to Mexico.

From Shenzhen to Mexico: healthcare technology is becoming another frontier of China–Latin America cooperation.

• The implications of Artificial Intelligence for intellectual property rights and dispute resolution.
One insight that particularly stood out to me:
Resolving an intellectual property dispute is not simply a matter of reaching an agreement. The outcome must also be clearly documented, legally sound, and structured to achieve its intended effect, including effective implementation or enforcement where applicable.
More broadly, this reinforces an important principle in intellectual property practice: effective protection goes beyond registration. It also depends on sound contractual safeguards, early dispute prevention, and carefully considered dispute resolution mechanisms.
My sincere appreciation to WIPO, the distinguished speakers, and the organizing team for facilitating this valuable international exchange. I also appreciated the opportunity to connect with fellow professionals from different countries and legal backgrounds.

From Neural Networks to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs): A Research Journey Spanning Nearly a Decade!

Research is a continuous journey of learning, exploration, and connecting ideas across disciplines.

My journey in machine learning began in 2017 during my postdoctoral research at Hiroshima University, Japan, when I worked on my first machine-learning research paper, "Machine Learning Algorithm for Autonomous Control of Walking Robot." 

The work involved developing a supervised learning algorithm using Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), backpropagation, and real-time pressure sensor data, with experimental hardware implementation for autonomous walking robot control.

During my Ph.D., my research focused on Graphene Nanoribbon (GNR) interconnect materials and physics-based mathematical modelling. The primary objective was to investigate and improve VLSI circuit performance in terms of propagation delay, power consumption, and chip area through advanced interconnect modelling.

These two research directions may initially appear different, but they gradually inspired me to explore a broader question:

Can we integrate the governing principles of physics with the learning capabilities of neural networks to address complex problems across multiple engineering and scientific disciplines?

After years of research, mathematical exploration, and interdisciplinary discussions, this vision has gradually evolved into our current research on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).

The exciting aspect of PINNs is their potential to establish a meaningful connection between several disciplines, including:

Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence
Physics and Chemistry
Mathematics and Biotechnology
Civil and Mechanical Engineering
Electronics and Electrical Engineering

Our two recent research papers on Physics-Informed Neural Networks represent an important outcome of this long research journey. 

I believe that integrating physical laws, mathematical formulations, and data-driven intelligence can open new research opportunities beyond conventional disciplinary boundaries.

For me, research is not merely about publishing papers; it is about connecting knowledge developed over time and transforming it into solutions for interdisciplinary challenges.

I was honoured to be invited by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea (MOFA) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) to speak and participate in the 25th ROK-UN Conference on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Issues, held in Seoul on 12–13 November 2026.

This year’s theme was “The Multifaceted Impacts and Implications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Disarmament, Non-Proliferation and Arms Control.”

🧬 Biosecurity and biological weapons

I delivered a presentation titled “Biosecurity and Bioweapons Prohibition in the Age of AI: Risks and Opportunities for Southeast Asia” during the panel on “AI and Chemical and Biological Weapons – Implications for Prohibition Regimes and Risk Reduction.”

I explored how AI can strengthen disease surveillance, outbreak preparedness, laboratory security and biological risk assessment, while also creating new dual-use and cyberbiosecurity risks. I highlighted the importance of ASEAN cooperation, responsible AI governance, stronger national biosecurity capacities and effective implementation of the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC). This is based on our biosecurity research program at RSIS | S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies . 

☢️ AI, nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation

I also had the opportunity to exchange insights on the implications of AI for nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation, particularly its potential impact on the implementation of key international instruments, including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), and Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone (NWFZ) treaties. Discussions considered how emerging AI applications could create new challenges and opportunities for treaty implementation, verification, monitoring, risk reduction and international cooperation.

🌐 Broadening the conversation on arms control

I was particularly delighted to see regional and international discussions on arms control and disarmament moving beyond traditional security insights. The inclusion of new-generation experts, greater attention to frontier technologies such as AI, and engagement with emerging actors from scientific, technological and private-sector communities are broadening the perspectives and expertise shaping disarmament conversations. This is essential to keeping arms control and disarmament frameworks relevant to a rapidly changing technological and security landscape.

🙏 My sincere thanks to MOFA of the Republic of Korea and UNODA for convening this important dialogue. It was a valuable opportunity to share research, exchange perspectives and explore how technological advances can be harnessed while safeguarding international peace and security.

Introducing CKCA Research OS Ω∞: Building the Architecture for Knowledge That Can Be Reconstructed, Evaluated, and Governed

What happens when human intelligence, artificial intelligence, institutions, research, and distributed knowledge must work together without losing context, provenance, accountability, or the ability to correct mistakes?

That is the problem I am addressing through CKCA Research OS Ω∞ — Constitutional Knowledge Coordination Architecture.

My work explores an architecture designed to coordinate knowledge across disciplines, intelligent systems, institutions, and knowledge holders while preserving the distinctions that matter:

• Research discovers.
• Evidence supports.
• Engineering implements.
• Evaluation verifies.
• Constitutional governance adopts.
• Stewardship preserves.

CKCA is organized around thirteen constitutional laws, five research tiers, fifteen lifecycle stages, and eight independent maturity dimensions.

Its foundational principles include:

Evidence Before Complexity.
Reconstruct Before Concluding.
Provenance by Default.
Context Before Generalization.
Disagreement Preservation.
Continuous Correctability.

The central proposition is straightforward: knowledge should not become institutional authority merely because an AI system generated it, a majority accepted it, or an organization repeated it.

Research findings and recommendations do not automatically authorize adoption or execution. Authority, evidence, decisions, and accountability must remain distinguishable.

I am currently developing the proposed v2.1 Draft 0.1 review through passage-level reconciliation, source attribution, and a separate review register. This is documentary architectural work—not a claim of completed implementation, certification, or institutional adoption.

I believe the next generation of intelligence infrastructure must do more than produce answers. It must preserve how conclusions were reached, what remains uncertain, who holds authority, and how decisions can be corrected.

The objective is not simply more intelligence. It is intelligence that can be examined, challenged, reconstructed, and responsibly governed.

This week, I reviewed a 2022 research paper:

“Business Intelligence and Analytics (BIA) Usage in the Banking Industry Sector: An Application of the TOE Framework.”

The study explores how technological, organisational, and environmental factors influence Business Intelligence and Analytics adoption in the banking sector.


🔍 Key research insights:

Data-related and technology-supporting infrastructure play an important role in analytics adoption.
Top-management support and organisational champions encourage analytics implementation.
Employee capabilities and talent management are important organisational considerations.

The study, based on responses from 120 employees at Arab Bank in Jordan, highlights that successful analytics adoption involves more than technology. Organisational readiness and external conditions matter too.

Before organisations can benefit from advanced AI-driven analytics, they need the right technological infrastructure, capable people, management support, and an environment that encourages adoption.

Does “customer” mean a contact or an account?
Can a deal have two owners?
What happens when the source system sends an empty value?

A plan that can't answer those questions isn't ready for a build.

Use AI to draft the process map, sure.
But make it produce an assumptions register, conflicting definitions, and the questions that need a human owner.

A beautiful answer is easy to generate.
A useful question can save weeks of rework.

Most enterprise AI safety still relies on probabilistic guardrails—training models to “behave” or wrapping them in text filters.

In high-consequence systems, behavioral alignment cannot fix an architectural privilege problem. When an autonomous agent holds execution authority across retry loops, even a tiny per-attempt failure probability compounds into substantial cumulative risk (the Regeneration Gap).

The fix isn’t a smarter prompt filter. It’s separating proposal from permission:

Existence ≠ Permission.

When a human-AI cockpit can initiate real-world actions, its cognitive interface may adapt—but its permission boundary must remain independently enforced: D(a) = DENY ⇒ Δ_external(a) = 0.

AI Automation: Moving from Hype to Business Value

An AI agent is software you give a goal. It works out the steps itself, using tools such as email, a CRM or search, and checks its own results as it goes.

Underneath, it runs on five parts: a model that reasons, tools it can call, instructions that describe the job, memory for what it needs to carry between steps, and limits on what it can do without approval. A hypothetical 12-person landscaping company shows the pattern: its agent reads a quote request, checks the price list and the crew calendar, drafts a quote, then rechecks the numbers before filing the draft for the owner to send.

Read access and the right to draft are a sensible starting point for any new agent. Write access gets earned once it has a track record on real work.
