💰 FUNDING YOUR STARTUP: HOW DO YOU GET THE CAPITAL TO GROW?

You have an idea.
You have a plan.
You may even have your first customers.
But when it's time to grow, one important question comes up:

Where will the money come from?

Startup funding isn't just about raising money. It's about understanding your business needs, choosing the right source of capital, and knowing when to raise it.

💡 6 KEY SOURCES OF STARTUP FUNDING

• 💵 BOOTSTRAPPING
Use your personal savings or business revenue to get started while maintaining greater ownership and control.

• 👼 ANGEL INVESTORS
Get early-stage capital from individuals who may also bring mentorship, industry connections, and strategic guidance.

• 📈 VENTURE CAPITAL
Raise investment from VC firms when your startup has the potential for significant growth and scalability.

• 🏛️ GRANTS & GOVERNMENT SCHEMES
Explore eligible government initiatives and grant programmes that support innovation, research, and entrepreneurship. Some offer non-dilutive funding, subject to their terms.

• 🤝 CROWDFUNDING
Raise money from a large number of people through suitable platforms and campaigns.

• 🏦 BANK LOANS & FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS
Access debt financing for eligible business needs, keeping repayment obligations and cash flow in mind.

🎯 HOW DO YOU CHOOSE THE RIGHT FUNDING OPTION?

Before approaching investors or applying for funding, ask yourself:
• What stage is my startup at?
• How much capital do I actually need?
• What will the money help me achieve?
• Am I ready to share equity or take on debt?
• Which funding options am I eligible for?

💡THE BIG LESSON

Not every startup needs venture capital.
The right funding option depends on your business model, growth stage, capital requirements, and long-term goals.

Remember:

❌ Don't raise money just because other startups are raising funds.

✅ Raise capital with a clear purpose, a realistic plan, and a strategy for using it effectively.

Funding is a tool for growth - not a measure of startup success. 🚀

Doughnut Economics Explained

Developed by economist Kate Raworth, doughnut economics offers a simple picture of a sustainable economy. Key ideas from this short video:

1. Social foundation: no one should fall short on essentials such as food, health and education.
2. Ecological ceiling: economic activity must stay within the planet's boundaries.
3. The safe and just space between the two rings is where societies can thrive.
4. Cities like Amsterdam are already applying the model to real policy.

Growth alone is not the goal; balance between human needs and planetary limits is.

Fundraising is not the goal. Building a sustainable and profitable business is. The right financing should follow to accelerate its growth.

I was glad to share some perspectives on The Fundraising Roadmap: From Seed to Exit with the cohort of The Reverse Innovation Cambodia by Techo Startup Center.

While fundraising and investment may sound like familiar conversations in the startup ecosystem, I wanted to bring a slightly different perspective to the discussion, drawing from what I have observed over the past two years at KUMPUL and KUMPUL Impact , working closely with entrepreneurs and leading entrepreneurship programmes across different stages of business growth.

One thing that has become increasingly clear to me: entrepreneurs should not become too fixated on raising capital. Before thinking about the next funding round, usiness owners need to strengthen their business fundamentals, understand their bottom line, build sustainable revenue streams, and, most importantly, be intentional about the game they choose to play.

I also believe that, whenever possible, external financing should be used to accelerate growth rather than sustain business-as-usual operations. Capital should help businesses scale, enter new markets, strengthen their capabilities, or unlock new opportunities, not become a permanent substitute for a viable business model and healthy cash flow.

And when external financing becomes necessary, venture capital is not the only answer.

There are other financing instruments worth exploring, from grants and revenue-based financing to debt, convertible instruments, and strategic capital. Depending on the business model and growth stage, these alternatives can sometimes be more effective without requiring founders to sacrifice too much ownership or control.

Capital is available, but the dynamics are changing. Investors are becoming more selective, while business owners are increasingly expected to demonstrate stronger fundamentals, clearer business models, and more disciplined growth strategies.

Perhaps the conversation should shift from "How do we raise our next round?" to "What kind of capital actually makes sense for the business we are building, and what will it help us achieve?"

Thank you, Sovireak Sath , for the opportunity to exchange ideas and learn from the entrepreneurs in the cohort. Always happy to share perspectives and learn from different startup ecosystems, especially across Southeast Asia.

One thing I’ve learned while working with founders is that a strong growth story is only one part of being ready for investment.

The other part is understanding the details that could affect execution.

For example, before starting a fundraise or acquisition discussion, I believe it’s worth asking: have we reviewed the contracts the business depends on?

Customer agreements, supplier arrangements, leases and licences may contain renewal dates, consent requirements or change-of-control provisions that need attention during a transaction.

A few questions I encourage founders to consider with their legal advisors:

• Which agreements are critical to revenue or operations?
• Could any require consent for the proposed transaction?
• Are important renewals approaching?
• Who is responsible for resolving an open issue, and by when?

The purpose isn’t to create more paperwork. It’s to identify important dependencies early, so they don’t become surprises when an investor is ready to move forward.

Investment readiness is not just about being ready to pitch. It’s also about being ready to execute.

TailBlaze's pitch takes the conversation into pet nutrition where Manaal Maniyar has found a void, where questions around differentiation, margins, customer acquisition and repeat purchases become central to the business case. 

Kwanzaa Lifestyle brings sustainability and corporate gifting into the room where Sainath Gurav, M.Sc., M.B.A. and Darsh Mehta found a huge void, prompting questions about repeat demand and the economics of expanding into direct-to-consumer sales.

Want to become an AI Engineer? 

Don't start with AI tools. 

Start with the fundamentals that make AI systems work.

Learning ChatGPT, LangChain, or AI agents is only one part of the journey.

To build real-world AI applications, you need a strong foundation in programming, mathematics, databases, backend engineering, cloud, and system architecture.

Think of AI Engineering as a progression, not a shortcut.

Here are 15 skill areas to focus on as you build your AI Engineering career. 

🟡 STAGE 1: Programming Fundamentals

Mathematics & Logical Thinking
Understand linear algebra, probability, statistics, and problem-solving.
C/C++ Fundamentals
Learn programming logic, memory management, and computational thinking.
Python Programming
Master Python, functions, libraries, OOP, and writing clean, reusable code.
Data Structures & Algorithms
Understand arrays, trees, graphs, sorting, searching, and algorithmic complexity.

🟡 STAGE 2: Software Engineering
OOP & Java
Learn object-oriented design and software engineering principles.
Web Development
Understand HTTP, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and how web applications work.
Databases
Learn SQL, PostgreSQL, NoSQL, data modelling, and query optimization.
APIs & Backend Development
Build services using REST APIs, FastAPI, authentication, and integrations.
Frontend Development with React
Learn how to build interactive interfaces for AI-powered applications.
Git & Practical Projects
Build real applications, use version control, and learn collaborative development.

🟡 STAGE 3: Cloud & System Architecture
Cloud Computing with AWS
Understand cloud infrastructure, storage, compute, networking, and deployment.
DevOps & CI/CD
Learn Docker, automation, testing, deployment pipelines, and monitoring.
Microservices & Kubernetes
Understand distributed systems, containers, orchestration, and scalability.

🟡 STAGE 4: AI Engineering
Machine Learning & Deep Learning
Understand model training, neural networks, embeddings, transformers, and model evaluation.
Modern AI Engineering
Move beyond traditional machine learning and learn how to build production-ready AI applications:

LLM APIs and prompt engineering
Function calling and structured outputs
RAG and vector databases
AI agents and agentic workflows
MCP and tool integrations
Model evaluation and observability
AI security, guardrails, and governance
Production deployment and inference optimization

One of the clearest signs of seniority in engineering? Not needing to be right.

A good question in a code review can expose an assumption you didn’t notice. Sometimes your approach is valid—you’ve thought it through, and it works. But valid doesn’t automatically mean best. Someone else may see the problem from a different angle and come up with a simpler or stronger solution.

And I think this is where seniority really shows. 

Can you separate your ego from your implementation? 
Can you say, "That makes more sense, let's change it"? 
Can you care more about the outcome than whose idea survives?

To me, that’s a core part of technical leadership. The goal isn’t to win the discussion; the goal is to leave it with a better solution.

Autism, Employment and Software Testing: Finding the Right Fit

Neurodivergent Employment in Ireland | Part 4 of 6

What jobs are autistic people suited to?

There isn't an "autistic job". Autistic people have different abilities, interests, personalities, educational backgrounds and support needs. The objective should be to match the individual, rather than their diagnosis, with work in which they have the interest and aptitude to succeed.

There is research suggesting that technology can provide a particularly engaging environment for some autistic people. A systematic review of 94 studies found that autistic people tended to be engaged when interacting with computers, while research into autism and STEM education has also demonstrated the potential for autistic students to develop skills in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

Software testing involves understanding how systems should work, testing their behaviour, identifying defects and documenting the results. For someone who enjoys logical problem-solving, structured investigation and working through problems methodically, it can be an interesting and rewarding career. However, it's important not to stereotype: being autistic doesn't automatically make somebody good at technology or software testing.

At Eirenauts, our approach is to look at whether an individual shows an interest and aptitude for software testing work. Training can then help develop that potential into professional software testing skills and the possibility of a rewarding career.

Don't match a diagnosis to a job. Match the individual to the right opportunity.

One builds for your roadmap. The other builds at the intersection of two.

Before hiring a software developer, ask these questions

Looking for someone to develop software for your business?
Before discussing pricing, programming languages or delivery dates, take a step back.
There are important questions worth asking:

1. Do they understand the problem the software is supposed to solve?
2. Can they explain their proposed approach in language you understand?
3. How will the software protect business and customer data?
4. How will the system be tested before deployment?
5. What happens when the software needs maintenance or improvement?
6. Will your organisation retain appropriate access, documentation and control?
Software development is not simply about writing code.

It involves understanding business requirements, designing usable systems, testing functionality, considering security and planning for long-term maintenance.
The right development partner should think beyond delivery.

Episode 11 | Trust & Customer Confidence
Why Trust Is the Ultimate Banking Advantage: Can Innovation Succeed Without It?
Banks are investing heavily in technology, artificial intelligence, digital experiences and new products.
Customers can transfer money in seconds, open accounts online, access financial services through mobile applications and receive increasingly personalised experiences.
But behind all this innovation, one fundamental expectation remains unchanged:
Customers need to trust their bank.
Think about it.
Would you use a banking application if you weren't confident your money was safe?
Would you accept an AI-generated financial recommendation if you didn't understand how it was produced?
Would you trust a bank that couldn't explain a transaction, resolve a complaint or communicate properly during an incident?
Technology can make banking faster.
Innovation can make banking smarter.
But neither automatically makes banking more trustworthy.
📌 What builds customer trust?
🔐 Security
Protecting customers, their money and their personal information.
🔎 Transparency
Making products, fees, decisions and processes understandable.
🤝 Reliability
Delivering consistent experiences and keeping promises.
💬 Communication
Being honest and proactive, particularly when things go wrong.
⚖️ Fairness
Ensuring products and decisions treat customers responsibly.
📌 The Product Manager's lens
I believe trust should be designed into banking products from the beginning.
It shouldn't be something we try to recover after a problem occurs.
Product Managers need to ask:
Are we making the customer experience genuinely safer?
Are our processes transparent?
Have we considered what happens when something fails?
Are we balancing convenience with appropriate controls?
And are we measuring customer confidence alongside commercial performance?
This requires collaboration between Product, Technology, Risk, Compliance and Operations.
Because trust isn't owned by one department.
It's created through the entire customer experience.
⭐ My personal focus
How banks transform customer needs and complex banking problems into better products, safer processes and better outcomes.
For me, this is one of the most important principles of modern Product Management.
We shouldn't measure success only by how quickly we launch, how many features we deliver or how much technology we implement.
We should consider whether customers feel confident using what we build.
Because in banking, trust isn't simply part of the customer relationship.
Trust IS part of the product.

Data Is Power. But Who Protects It?

🔐 Cybersecurity, Artificial Intelligence & Data: The New Frontline of Digital Banking
💳 Digital banking has transformed the way we manage money. Payments, transfers, investments and financial services are now just a few clicks away.

But behind this convenience lies a growing challenge: How do financial institutions protect the data and trust that make digital banking possible?

🌐 Why is cybersecurity so important?
Digital banks rely heavily on cloud infrastructure, APIs, mobile applications and interconnected platforms. These technologies create new opportunities, but also expand the potential attack surface.

Identity theft, phishing, unauthorized access, payment fraud and data breaches are just some of the risks financial institutions must continuously address.

🤖 Where does AI come into the picture?
Artificial Intelligence is changing both sides of cybersecurity. On one hand, it helps financial institutions detect unusual transactions, identify suspicious behavior, recognize potential fraud patterns and respond to threats faster. On the other hand, cybercriminals can also use AI to create more sophisticated phishing campaigns, impersonate identities through deepfakes and automate social engineering attacks.

📊 And what about Data?
This is where Data Analytics becomes essential. Security systems need to analyze large volumes of information, identify anomalies, understand customer behavior and detect patterns that could indicate fraudulent activity. The quality, accuracy and governance of data directly influence the reliability of these systems.

However, collecting more data is not enough. Financial institutions must also ensure that information is protected, responsibly processed and used in compliance with privacy regulations.

🔎 My takeaway:
Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT responsibility. It is a strategic business priority. AI provides new capabilities, Data provides the intelligence, and Cybersecurity provides the protection.

Ultimately, the future of digital banking will depend not only on how innovative financial institutions become, but also on how effectively they protect the trust of their customers.

Because in digital finance, trust is an asset. And data security is one of the foundations that protects it.

Ignite, day 1: AI as the next operating system for the enterprise

My strongest takeaway from the first day in San Francisco: AI is becoming an operating layer connecting people, knowledge, applications and execution.

The event illustrated a shift towards agents coordinating work across business processes. For leaders, three priorities stand out.

Value. The opportunity is to redesign how work gets done: faster onboarding, fewer unresolved exceptions and more capacity to serve clients. Our people’s expertise and institutional knowledge will be essential to making this work.

Control. One concrete example was a pilot in which agents negotiated a US Treasury bill trade within predefined limits. Human traders retained approval, while execution followed existing systems and controls. A useful illustration of how autonomy can grow within clear boundaries. 

Economics. Falling model costs expand the possibilities. The investment case must capture the full cost of integration, oversight and operation—and measure cost per successful business outcome. Model choice, spending discipline and flexibility across providers become executive decisions.

I leave encouraged by the direction. The discussion increasingly brings capability, transparency and accountability together. The opportunity is to translate that progress into better services, stronger decisions and measurable value.

As AI takes on more work, how should we evolve the way we delegate, measure performance and retain control?

#ArtificialIntelligence #Leadership #ClientExperience

As we approach 2027, I believe the retail AI industry needs to prepare for a significant shift in expectations.

The conversation has centered on what artificial intelligence can accomplish. Autonomous scanning robots, computer vision, and advanced retail intelligence platforms have demonstrated extraordinary technological capabilities.

Retail executives want measurable ROI. Employees want to understand how technology affects their future. Consumers want transparency. And technology providers must be prepared to address all three.

The companies that begin preparing today may be the ones best positioned to lead tomorrow.

Artificial Intelligence Driven Transformation of 3D Concrete Printing in Architecture: A Systematic Review
This research explores how Artificial Intelligence is transforming architectural applications of 3D Concrete Printing (3DCP), particularly across three key areas:
• AI-driven design and form generation
• Material and structural performance optimisation
• Fabrication monitoring and quality assessment
Through a systematic review of the existing literature, we examined how machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks and computer vision are being applied across different stages of the 3DCP workflow.
The findings highlight the potential of AI to improve material efficiency, printability and fabrication quality, while also identifying challenges related to data availability, standardisation and real-world implementation.

As Artificial Intelligence continues to reshape how organizations operate and deliver value, understanding how to manage AI initiatives has become an increasingly important skill for project managers and business leaders.
The “Introduction to Cognitive Project Management in AI (CPMAI)™” eLearning course, offered by the Project Management Institute (PMI), is a useful starting point for anyone interested in understanding the unique challenges of AI project management and exploring the CPMAI methodology.
Unlike traditional project management approaches, AI initiatives involve uncertainty, experimentation, data dependencies, model performance, and continuous learning. The CPMAI methodology addresses these challenges through a structured, iterative approach built around six key phases:
1. Business Understanding: Defining the business problem, objectives, expected value, and project feasibility.
2. Data Understanding: Identifying, exploring, and assessing the availability, quality, and relevance of data.
3. Data Preparation: Cleaning, transforming, and preparing data for AI model development.
4. Model Development: Selecting, building, training, and refining AI models.
5. Model Evaluation: Evaluating model performance, reliability, and alignment with business objectives.
6. Model Operationalization: Deploying AI solutions into real-world operations, supported by governance, monitoring, and continuous improvement.
One of the most important principles behind this approach is that successful AI projects are not just about building better models; they are about solving the right business problems, working with the right data, and translating AI capabilities into measurable business value.
For project managers, PMO professionals, Agile practitioners, and business leaders looking to expand their understanding of AI, this introductory course is a valuable opportunity to explore a structured approach to managing AI initiatives.
A good starting point for connecting Project Management with the evolving world of Artificial Intelligence.

It was a pleasure speaking with  Calvin Lewis Bay News 9 about the Citrus County Sheriff's Office's integration of an AI system to handle non-emergency 911 calls.

My contribution to the discussion focused on the potential risks associated with this type of technology and its deployment: as with almost any AI implementation, there are legitimate concerns that need to be acknowledged and addressed. At the same time, in my opinion this is a good example of how AI can be harnessed to create significant value.

The reason is that the system is being introduced in a context where it can potentially improve efficiency and free up human resources, while the nature of the calls allows for a relatively controlled environment in which to evaluate its performance. Importantly, the system also has the ability to identify situations that require human intervention, which helps address some of the risks associated with relying on AI for this type of task.

This is a sensible approach to AI adoption: identifying a use case where the potential benefits are meaningful, the risks can with a high degree of likelihood be managed, and human oversight can remain part of the process.

‏USF Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing‏

Agentic AI in the Workplace: What Happens When Technology Begins Completing Tasks Independently?

Traditional AI tools often respond to questions or generate content.

Agentic AI introduces another capability: systems designed to plan and complete multistep tasks with varying levels of independence.

For example, an AI agent may gather information, update records, prepare reports, or coordinate workflows using connected tools.

This creates opportunities for greater efficiency.

However, it also introduces new risks when systems can take actions rather than simply provide recommendations.

Before deploying AI agents, organizations should establish:

✅ Clearly defined tasks and permitted actions.

✅ Limits on system access to sensitive information.

✅ Human approval for consequential decisions or transactions.

✅ Monitoring of automated activity.

✅ Procedures to stop, correct, or reverse inappropriate actions.

✅ Accountability for errors and unexpected results.

Organizations must distinguish between tasks AI can safely complete independently and decisions requiring human approval.

Leadership Takeaway: The more independently technology can operate, the more important clear boundaries, oversight, and accountability become.

Engagement Question: Would you trust an AI agent to complete workplace tasks independently, or should human approval remain part of every significant action?

Evaluating AI agents gets complicated quickly.

A workflow can finish successfully while producing the wrong result. It can also produce a correct result through excessive retries, expensive tool calls or substantial human intervention.

I find it useful to separate four concepts:

• Task: the work, context and acceptance criteria.
• Target: the executable system being evaluated.
• Trajectory: the record of what happened during execution.
• Evaluation: the checks and judgements applied to the outcome and the trajectory.

These distinctions help us evaluate individual steps and the overall outcome, understand failures, and compare different approaches against the same expectations.

They also influence how we build. Capturing trajectories, costs, timing and failure states needs to be considered from the start.

That’s the argument behind my article: define success early, and design the system so we can gather the evidence to assess it.

What if AI changes not just how we work, but how work is designed?

Consider a customer request that requires information, controls, analysis, expertise and a decision.

These activities are often organized into a sequence, with different people, systems and responsibilities contributing along the way.

When introducing AI, a natural starting point is to ask which steps could be accelerated or automated.

But another possibility is worth exploring.

What if we reconsidered the building blocks themselves?

Information gathering and analysis could become more closely connected.

Controls could be embedded differently across the activity.

Experts could contribute to an evolving analysis rather than waiting for a completed handover.

And AI could help explore alternatives as new information, constraints or expertise become available.

The opportunity is therefore not limited to improving individual steps.

It may also change the way work is assembled.

How information, controls and expertise come together.

How people and systems interact.

How decisions progressively take shape.

Not every activity needs to be redesigned. Some will benefit from targeted improvements. Others may offer opportunities for a more fundamental transformation.

The starting point remains the outcome we want to achieve.

The opportunity is not simply to make each step more intelligent. It is to rethink how the steps come together.

#ArtificialIntelligence #OperatingModel #BusinessTransformation

Supporting Client AI Prototyping Part 2

In the first post in this series, I explored encouraging clients to experiment with artificial intelligence while still providing honest engineering advice. The next challenge is making that advice useful when we see something differently. Ultimately, our goal is creating something wonderful together.

A broad statement like "this isn’t ready for production" doesn’t explain the concern or give us much to work through together. When I question a proposed design, I want us to be discussing what the solution needs to do, not defending who built it.

I’d rather identify the behavior we need, the assumption we’re making, and what we need to test.

For me, a constructive technical review should make a few things clear:

• What outcome are we trying to protect? 
• What specific behavior or assumption concerns us? 
• What is the consequence if that assumption is wrong? 
• What evidence would help us decide how to proceed?

That last question matters. Engineering judgment needs to be open to examination too. If I recommend a different approach, I should be able to explain the reason and what would change my recommendation.

Not every concern calls for a redesign. We might need a focused test, a clearer requirement, or an explicit limit on where the prototype will be used. The goal isn’t to win an argument about the implementation. It’s to agree on what people need to be able to rely on, then choose an approach that supports it.

What question or technique helps you turn a disagreement about an implementation into a productive discussion about the outcome?

Three mistakes businesses make when implementing AI  and how to avoid them.

AI adoption is growing, but adopting AI tools without a clear implementation strategy can create inefficiencies rather than solve them.
Here are three mistakes businesses should pay attention to:
1. Starting with the tool instead of the problem.
Not every business challenge requires an AI solution. Start by identifying a repetitive task, operational bottleneck or genuine business problem. Then determine whether AI is the right solution.
2. Feeding AI disorganised or incomplete information.
The quality of AI-generated results depends significantly on the quality of the information and instructions provided. Poor inputs can lead to inaccurate or inconsistent outputs.
3. Removing human oversight.
AI can assist with communication, content creation and business processes, but important outputs should still be reviewed. Automation should support human decision-making, not eliminate accountability.
A better approach:
Identify one real business problem.
Organise and validate your information.
Build a relevant AI workflow.
Maintain human review and accountability.
AI implementation is not simply about having the latest tools. It's about using the right tools to solve the right problems.

Can the model do something impressive?

It does not answer the question that matters on a difficult operating day:

Can our company run, govern, and recover this system?

Before choosing an AI implementation partner, ask them to put four artifacts on the table:

• A process map that includes the exceptions, not only the happy path
• A decision-rights matrix showing what the AI may do and where a person remains accountable
• An evaluation and recovery plan covering bad data, unavailable systems, incorrect outputs, and unauthorized actions
• A handover package with runbooks, administrative access, change control, training, and clear internal owners

If those artifacts do not exist, you are still evaluating a promise—not an operating capability.

I was exploring two emerging technologies: artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and computer vision, and blockchain.

Both intrigued me. 

But I could see a clearer path for AI to solve problems that affected people’s everyday lives. That’s where I chose to focus.

I’ve since worked on AI implementations across healthcare , transportation, financial services, and the public sector.

Along the way, my CTO diaries have filled up with lessons about what it takes to make AI useful:

1. Start with the use case.
Name the problem, the person experiencing it, and the decision you want to improve before choosing the technology.

2. Build responsibility into the design.
Privacy, governance, testing, and oversight need to shape development from the beginning.

3. Make explanations useful.
People need to understand why a system flagged something and what evidence supports it, especially when a decision may face scrutiny in court.

3. Treat data readiness as foundational.
Access, quality, context, and permissions determine what a solution can reliably do.

4. Design around the actual workflow.
Spend time with the people doing the work. Their constraints should shape the solution.

5. Give human reviewer a clear purpose.
Define who examines an output, what they need to verify, and who has authority to act.
Measure outcomes.

6. Establish a baseline. Track whether AI improves review time, decision quality, or service delivery.

7. Test beyond the demo.

Real implementation includes exceptions, incomplete data, integration, monitoring, and someone accountable for keeping it working.

Not Every AI Use Case Deserves a Budget. Here's How to Decide.
AI is exciting. But excitement doesn't equal business value. One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is investing in AI solutions before determining whether they're solving the right problem. Just because AI can do something doesn't mean your business should invest in it. Before approving your next AI initiative, ask a few questions: 

🎯 1. Business Value: What measurable problem are we solving? Will this reduce costs, increase revenue, or improve customer experience?
⚙️ 2. Implementation Effort: How difficult will this be to implement and integrate into existing workflows?
📊 3. Data Readiness: Do we have the quality, accessible data needed to make this successful?
🛡️ 4. Risk & Governance: What are the security, compliance, and operational risks?
⏱️ 5. Time to Value: How quickly can we demonstrate meaningful results?

Here's a practical example: A customer service team is considering two AI initiatives:
Option A: An AI chatbot that handles routine customer inquiries.
Option B: An AI-powered analytics solution that predicts customer churn.

Both have potential. But which one should receive funding first? The answer depends on business priorities, implementation readiness, expected ROI, and risk—not which technology sounds more impressive.

💡 My takeaway: The best AI strategy doesn't start with selecting tools. It starts with identifying and prioritizing the right business opportunities.

What matters most when your organization evaluates an AI investment: ROI, speed, or strategic impact?

For Dine, we've developed 48 scripted test cases covering everyday requests and adversarial inputs, including prompt injection attempts and fake prices.

Our latest results show 25 out of 26 everyday cases passing, all 22 adversarial cases passing, and zero invented prices or meals.

We've also optimized our search workflow, reducing model calls from approximately seven per request to an average of 1.5, with median response times of 8.9 seconds or less.

And when the model is unavailable, Dine falls back to keyword search, allowing users to still access real meals, prices, and allergen warnings.

We're building with the understanding that a useful AI system must be tested, efficient, and resilient beyond its ideal operating conditions.

The most fundable startups in 2026 are not always the best ones.

They are the most visible ones.

I have watched genuinely brilliant founders spend eighteen months building something real, technically defensible, commercially promising — and raise nothing. Not because the idea was wrong. Because nobody who could write a cheque ever knew they existed.

Visibility is not vanity. At the pre-seed and seed stage, being known is part of the product.

The founder who publishes, who shows their thinking, who lets the right people see what they are building before a formal raise — that founder has warmed the room before they ever walked into it.

The founder who builds in silence and then sends cold decks into the void is asking investors to make a cold decision about a stranger.

Here is the uncomfortable truth about early fundraising:

Your idea does not sell itself. Your story does. And your story cannot travel if it lives only in your head and a pitch deck nobody has seen.

The round does not start when you send the first email. It starts the moment the right person hears what you are building and thinks — I want to know more about that.

So here is the question worth sitting with:

If the right investor searched for what you are building today — would they find you?

If not — that is the problem to solve before the deck, before the data room, before the ask.

We are building a place where early-stage founders can change that.

a.n.d.a. is a discovery platform for pre-seed and seed-stage founders raising $100K–$5M. If you are building something ambitious and the right people do not know you exist yet — this is where that changes.

List your startup here: https://anda.ericfrank.co/

And in the comments — introduce yourself:

What are you building, what problem does it solve, and how much are you raising?

Let's find out what is being built right now that the world has not heard about yet. 👇

$120 million in funding. A promising idea. An innovative product.

And ultimately, a failed business.

What went wrong?

In this excerpt from today's Pinnacle Process Group Basecamp Workshop, I share the story of Juicero and an important lesson for entrepreneurs.

Support is not validation.

You can have enthusiastic investors, encouraging friends and family, and a product that everyone agrees sounds like a great idea.

But there's a fundamental difference between people believing in your business and customers demonstrating that they need what you're offering.

Funding provides resources.

Encouragement provides motivation.

Validation provides evidence.

And without that evidence, even $120 million might not be enough.

Before asking how to fund your idea, consider whether you've done enough to validate it.

Are you building something people admire, or something customers actually need?

Integrating artificial intelligence into mobile applications changes how software interacts with users, yet poor architecture often ruins the experience. Many teams try to run heavy models directly on mobile devices without optimizing memory and battery consumption. When an app heats up or lags during inference, users uninstall it immediately.

I treat AI integration as a core architectural challenge rather than an afterthought. We design hybrid pipelines that balance fast on device processing with scalable cloud computing. By using lightweight models and edge optimization, we keep response times low even on standard hardware. In enterprise mobile apps, this approach enables real time personalization, voice recognition, and visual data analysis without network delays. AI also accelerates our internal development workflow by automating repetitive code generation and regression testing. Instead of spending months on basic setup, our engineers focus on security, data privacy, and smooth user interfaces. Reliable mobile AI requires strict control over data flows and continuous performance monitoring after release. The goal is to deliver intelligent features that feel native and effortless on any screen.

AI innovation is increasingly constrained by how quickly systems can move data, not just how fast they can compute. This shift is driving new approaches to processor architecture, memory design, and hardware-software co-optimization. Have you ever wondered why some salespeople build long-term relationships with customers while others focus only on closing deals?

Ask the right questions to understand the customer's real needs instead of immediately presenting your product.

Sales management involves planning, organising, directing and controlling the activities of a sales force to help an organisation achieve its sales, profit and growth objectives.

In simpler terms, sales management is the process of managing the people, activities, resources and customer relationships involved in selling a company's products or services.

What are the objectives of Sales Management?

There are several objectives, but let's look at four important ones:

1. Achieving Sales Volume

One major objective is to ensure that the organisation meets its sales targets and sells the expected quantity of products or services.

2. Promoting Business Growth

Sales management helps an organisation expand its market share, reach new customers and strengthen its position in the marketplace.

3. Generating Customers

It helps businesses identify potential customers (prospects) and convert them into actual buyers through effective selling strategies.

4. Reducing Sales Costs and Improving Performance

Effective sales management helps organisations use their resources efficiently, minimise unnecessary selling expenses and improve the productivity of their sales team.

A Practical Example:

Imagine a phone and laptop business in Port Harcourt.

The business owner sets monthly sales targets, assigns responsibilities to sales representatives, monitors their performance and develops strategies to attract more customers.

All these activities are part of sales management.

Final Thought:

Selling a product is important, but managing the entire selling process is what helps a business achieve sustainable growth.

Sales Productivity Hack # 12

Are you talking more than your customer during sales meetings?

Many sales professionals spend most of their time explaining product features, presenting solutions and talking about their company's capabilities.

But here's the problem: The more you talk without understanding the customer's needs, the harder it becomes to recommend the right solution.

Here's a simple productivity hack: Prepare 5 Discovery Questions Before Every Sales Meeting.

Start with these:

1. What are the biggest challenges you're currently facing?
2. How are you addressing these challenges today?
3. What impact are these challenges having on your business?
4. What would an ideal solution look like for you?
5. What factors will influence your buying decision?

Listen carefully. Don't rush to pitch.

The result? Better understanding of customer needs, more relevant solutions and shorter, more meaningful sales conversations.

Remember, great salespeople don't win by talking more. They win by asking better questions and listening carefully.

One of the quickest ways a SaaS business can grow itself into trouble is spending more to win customers than those customers are ever worth..

A SaaS company can grow every year without signing a single new customer.

The number that tells you if yours can is net revenue retention, or NRR 👇

How to calculate it this week:
→ Take every customer you had a year ago.
→ Add up what that same group pays you today.
→ Divide by what they paid back then.

An example. Say that group paid you $1M a year.
↳ Some left and took $100K with them.
↳ Some cut back, another $50K.
↳ Others added seats and bought more, $250K.

Now that same group pays $1.1M. That's 110% NRR.

Above 100%, your customers grow your revenue for you, and every new deal lands on top.

Below 100%, you have to replace what leaks out before you can grow at all.

A survey of over a thousand private SaaS companies found the median is 101%. Just over the line.

Here's the part most founders overlook. Buyers pay for this number.

Software Equity Group's 2025 Annual SaaS Report looked at public SaaS companies by NRR and their median revenue multiple at sale:
• Under 90% NRR: 1.2x
• 100-110% NRR: 6.0x
• Over 120% NRR: 11.7x

Two ways to push yours up:
• Price so customers pay more as they use more.
• Make upgrading easy.

Churn shrinks you quietly.

Expansion grows you quietly.

This is one challenge SaaS businesses must anticipate as they scale.

Growing your customer base is exciting, but can your customer success and support operations keep up?

In SaaS, growth requires more than acquiring new customers. It requires scalable processes, the right tools, adequate support structures, and people who can maintain a consistent customer experience.

Because acquiring more customers is one thing. Ensuring they adopt your product, achieve value from it, and remain satisfied is another.

Growth should increase your reach, not reduce the quality of your customer experience.

P.S. More customers are a sign of progress, but a growing SaaS business must also grow its capacity to onboard, support, and retain them. Otherwise, that growth may become the very reason customers churn.

Most board presentations report #NetRevenueRetention (#NRR) as one blended number.

1. NRR by acquisition cohort

2. NRR by the promise that closed the deal

>> And when customers don't realise the value they were sold, expansion becomes an uphill battle.

Now consider the second-order effect.
NRR falls → Cost pressures rise → Customer Success budgets get cut → Retention deteriorates further → EBITDA improves temporarily.
>> The board sees better margins. But the underlying revenue engine is weakening.

That's not sustainable growth. That's margin improvement at the expense of future revenue.

Here's the distinction SaaS leaders need to understand:
- Repricing can improve the NRR number.
- Cost optimisation can improve EBITDA.
>> But neither necessarily improves the value customers realise from your product.

And without realised value, sustainable retention and expansion remain elusive.

In this video, I break down why looking beyond the blended NRR number matters, what leadership teams should investigate, and why the real fix may lie much earlier in the #CustomerLifecycle.

A question for CEOs, CROs and CS leaders:
When your NRR last declined, what did your leadership team fix first?
>> Pricing? Customer Success costs? Retention processes? Or the original promise made to the customer?

A SaaS Product can become more valuable to its customers while becoming less scalable for the company behind it.

Deep integration into customer workflows can strengthen retention, support expansion and create lasting competitive advantages.

But every new customer requirement creates a Product decision.

Should it become part of the core platform? Be supported through configuration or integrations? Or remain a customer-specific solution?

Each choice affects more than functionality.

It shapes implementation effort, architectural complexity, maintenance costs and the ability to serve future customers.

The challenge is no to eliminate customization.

Some customer-specific capabilities justify their cost through premium pricing, strategic relationships or opportunities to serve a broader market.

Others create obligations that accumulate faster than the value they generate.

For SaaS leaders, the important question is not simply how deeply a Product becomes embedded in customer operations.

It is whether that embeddedness creates value the business can capture and deliver efficiently as it grows.

Customer embeddedness can protect revenue, but only scalable economics turn it into a durable competitive advantage.

In 2027, every SaaS business becomes a startup again

Coming away from last week's CPO Track®, hearing how established organisations across telecoms, healthcare and insurance are rethinking their strategies in the era of AI, I couldn't help but apply the same lens to my world of enterprise SaaS

Regardless of ARR, customer base or brand recognition, the game is changing. Adding a few AI features to an existing product isn't reinvention. It's incremental improvement in a market being fundamentally redefined

Established SaaS businesses have an advantage. Revenue to fund their next chapter, customers to experiment and evolve with, and infrastructure that startups are still building

But those advantages only matter if they're willing to think and operate like startups again.
As we head into 2027, every SaaS leadership team should be asking:

 👉 Product: If we started from scratch today, would we build what we're selling?
 👉 GTM: Is our go-to-market model built for the market ahead or the one we're leaving behind?
 👉 Organisation: Are we structured to innovate and execute at the pace required?

The winners won't necessarily be the newest companies or the biggest incumbents. They'll be the ones willing to challenge what they've built and reinvent themselves before someone else does

2027 is going to be fascinating. The playing field is being reset.

Here's the digital growth framework I'd implement for a SaaS company.

01. Market & Competitor Intelligence
• Identify ideal customer profiles (ICP).
• Research customer pain points and buying intent.

02. SEO & Search Demand Capture

03. AIO + GEO + AEO Strategy

04. Conversion-Focused Content

THE GROWTH EQUATION
Search Visibility + AI Search Presence + Demand Generation + Conversion Optimization + Lead Nurturing = A Connected SaaS Growth Strategy.

Great SaaS products rarely fail because of weak features. They stall—or churn six months after signature—because they cannot cleanly connect to the systems running the customer’s business.
Across multiple scaling stages, I have seen talented engineering organizations hit the exact same growth wall for this reason.
Look at how modern enterprise software actually gets used. A finance platform is only as valuable as its sync with the customer’s ERP, billing, and banking infrastructure. An analytics platform is blind without reliable pipelines from the systems where work actually happens. Without seamless connectivity, you are asking an enterprise buyer to adopt another isolated silo—and at renewal time, silos are the first thing cut.
The trap most growing companies fall into is treating integrations as one-off implementation work rather than core architecture.
Sales closes an enterprise logo. Engineering builds a custom connector, writes a bespoke mapping, and patches edge-case exceptions post-launch. Repeat.
In the early days, that feels like customer obsession. At scale, it becomes technical debt disguised as customer onboarding—quietly draining your best engineers and slowing down the core product roadmap.
The inflection point for a mature technology organization is elevating integrations from back-office plumbing to a first-class pillar of product strategy:
• Architect a reusable integration layer rather than maintaining brittle, point-to-point connectors.
• Enforce canonical data models so every new customer does not require reinventing the schema.
• Centralize observability and error handling before your customer support team becomes the alerting system.
• Deploy AI where it genuinely earns its keep—accelerating schema mapping, flagging data drift, and triaging anomalies before a customer ever notices.
When connectivity is engineered as a core product capability, the return shows up directly on the P&L: faster time-to-value, lower support overhead, and stronger net dollar retention. Your product stops being another standalone login and becomes embedded in how the customer operates.
At scale, architecture is never just about keeping the lights on. It is one of the strongest levers a company has for defensibility and growth.
For fellow technology and product leaders: how is your organization structured around this today—owned by a dedicated platform team, or still absorbed as custom onboarding work?

Your SaaS business is growing its revenue from existing customers.

But here’s a question:

Are your existing customers actually staying and spending more, or are you simply replacing the revenue you’re losing?

There’s a difference.

And understanding it starts with two important customer success metrics: Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) and Net Revenue Retention (NRR).

Let’s break them down.

1. Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)

GRR measures how much recurring revenue your business retains from existing customers over a given period, excluding expansion revenue.

It accounts for revenue lost through cancellations and downgrades.

In simple terms, it answers:

“How much of the revenue we started with did we actually keep?”

2. Net Revenue Retention (NRR)

NRR measures how much recurring revenue your business retains from existing customers after accounting for cancellations, downgrades, and expansion revenue.

Expansion can come from customers upgrading their plans, purchasing additional seats, or adopting more services.

It answers:

“After accounting for revenue lost and revenue gained from existing customers, how much recurring revenue do we have left?”

Here’s a simple example.

Imagine your SaaS business starts the month with $100,000 in recurring revenue from existing customers.

During that month:

* $10,000 is lost through cancellations.
* $5,000 is lost through downgrades.
* $20,000 is gained through upgrades and expansion.

Your results:

GRR = 85%

NRR = 105%

Your business retained 85% of its starting recurring revenue before expansion, while expansion revenue helped bring net revenue retention to 105%.

Notice something?

Your business lost revenue from existing customers, but expansion more than offset those losses.

That’s why looking at NRR alone doesn’t tell the entire story.

A strong NRR is encouraging, but GRR helps reveal how well you’re retaining the revenue you already have.

Where does Customer Success come in?

A proactive CSM doesn’t wait until renewal conversations to think about revenue retention.

They monitor product adoption, identify declining engagement, understand changing customer needs, demonstrate ROI, and uncover opportunities to help customers get more value.

A TAM can also help address technical barriers, integrations, and configuration challenges that affect product usage and perceived value.

Because expansion should come from customers receiving more value, not simply being sold a bigger package.

Founders and SaaS leaders: Are you measuring both GRR and NRR, or are you celebrating expansion revenue without examining what you’re losing underneath?

If your business wants to improve customer retention, understand churn drivers, and build stronger recurring revenue, let’s connect.

Customer success should contribute to sustainable growth, not just manage relationships.

One of the biggest mistakes salespeople make is trying to sell before they understand the customer.

After years of working in sales and training sales teams, I have learned that asking better questions often leads to better sales conversations.

Too often, salespeople focus on explaining product features before understanding what the customer needs.

But customers do not always care about what your product can do.

They care about what it can do for them.

Here are four ways to improve your sales conversations:

1. Ask before presenting. Learn what the customer wants to accomplish before discussing your solution.
2. Listen for problems. Pay attention to what is frustrating the customer or preventing them from reaching their goals.
3. Connect value to their needs. Explain how your product or service addresses the problems they shared.
4. Confirm understanding. Ask whether your solution addresses their concerns before moving forward.

For example, instead of immediately explaining why your product is better than the competition, ask:

“What is the biggest challenge you are trying to solve?”

That one question can change the direction of the entire conversation.

Great salespeople do not just know how to sell. They know how to help customers buy.

The next time you speak with a customer, spend less time presenting and more time understanding.

Sales is not just about convincing people to buy. It is about understanding human behaviour, identifying needs, building trust and making buying decisions easier.
There are certain truths about sales that separate average sales representatives from exceptional sales professionals.
Here are secrets worth understanding.
1. Customers Don't Buy Products; They Buy Solutions.
People are less interested in what your product does than in how it improves their lives or businesses.
Secret: Stop selling features. Start selling outcomes.
2. The Person Who Asks the Best Questions Often Wins the Sale.
Great salespeople don't dominate conversations. They ask intelligent questions that uncover customers' actual problems.
For example:
What challenges are you currently experiencing?
How is this affecting your business?
What have you tried to solve the problem?
What would an ideal solution look like?
This is where consultative selling becomes powerful.
3. People Buy Emotionally and Justify Logically.
A customer may desire a product because of convenience, security, status or peace of mind. They then justify the purchase using price, quality and value.
Secret: Understand both the emotional and logical reasons behind a buying decision.
4. Silence Can Close Deals.
Many salespeople lose opportunities because they talk too much.
After presenting your offer, give the prospect room to think and respond.
Sometimes, the most powerful sales technique is knowing when to stop talking.
5. Follow-Up Is Where the Real Money Is.
Not every interested prospect will buy immediately.
Some need:
More information.
Time to consider.
Approval from management.
Financial readiness.
Reassurance.

What else can you add as a sales strategist?

You’ll build trust, make the conversation more relevant, and see whether your solution is the right fit.

One of the most important lessons I've learned throughout my experience in Sales, Customer Service, and Retention is that selling is not just about knowing the product or presenting its benefits. It's also about understanding emotions.

Think about it:

Rejection: Not every customer will say yes. Learning not to take rejection personally is essential to staying motivated.
Frustration: Some conversations can be challenging. The ability to remain calm, listen, and understand the customer's concerns can completely change the direction of a conversation.
Confidence: Customers can often sense when you are unsure. Knowing your product and believing in the value you offer helps build trust.
Pressure: Targets, KPIs, and expectations are part of sales. However, allowing pressure to control your behavior can negatively affect the customer experience.
Empathy: Sometimes, the customer doesn't need another sales pitch. They need someone who understands their situation and can offer a solution that makes sense.

So, how do we manage these emotions?

Listen before responding.
Separate rejection from your personal value.
Focus on solutions instead of arguments.
Understand the customer's perspective.
Stay focused on the value you provide, not just the sale.
After years of working in sales, customer service, collections, and retention, I've learned that emotional intelligence is just as important as product knowledge and sales techniques.

A successful sales professional doesn't need to control the customer. They need to learn how to manage themselves, understand the customer, and guide the conversation in the right direction.

What's your experience? What emotion do you think is the hardest to manage during a sales conversation?

“I know there's a lot on this slide…”

Stop.

If you know there is too much on the slide, why are you showing it?

Salespeople often mistake detail for credibility.

But buyers have limited attention and limited working memory.

Complexity creates mental effort.
Mental effort can create uncertainty.
Uncertainty can increase perceived risk.

That is why clarity matters commercially.

One practical rule: One slide. One job.

Another: Do not make the buyer identify the signal inside the noise.

Tell them what matters.
“The most important point here is…”
“Of these five capabilities, two are relevant to your problem…”
“There are three things I want you to remember…”

Expertise is not demonstrated by making complex things sound complicated.

Expertise is demonstrated by making complexity understandable.

People hate being sold to. Yet every business depends on sales.

So why do we resist someone trying to sell us something, even when their offer might be exactly what we need?

Psychology has an explanation: psychological reactance.

When we feel someone is trying to control our decisions, we can experience an urge to resist. We may reject an offer before we’ve even considered its value.

For business owners, understanding this changes how we approach sales. Instead of telling people what they need, we can ask questions, understand their problems, explain our offer and leave them free to decide.

But there’s another side to this.

Many business owners know exactly how important selling is. They have a good service, know who their customers are and understand what they need to do. Still, they hesitate to reach out, follow up or make an offer.

Why? Because rejection can feel personal.

And here’s something worth remembering: when someone resists your offer, they may be reacting to the feeling of being sold to rather than the value of what you’re offering.

Understanding the psychology of rejection can change both how you sell and how confidently you approach the next opportunity.

Your next payment may not be initiated by a human. Is your payment platform ready?
For decades, fintech innovation has focused on making payments faster, cheaper and more seamless.
But we are approaching a fundamental shift.
What happens when the customer is no longer the one initiating the payment — an AI agent is?
Recent developments are making this increasingly real:
🔹 OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet enables AI agents to complete purchases with user approval.
🔹 Visa, BILL and Billtrust are piloting AI agents executing previously approved B2B invoice payments.
🔹 EMVCo is exploring standards to establish and manage customer intent in agent-initiated transactions.
These developments raise a fascinating architectural question.
A transaction can be authenticated, authorized and successfully settled. But how do we prove that an AI agent acted within the customer's actual intent?
Consider an AI agent instructed to pay approved supplier invoices.
What prevents it from paying a duplicate invoice, exceeding a spending limit, or transferring money to an unauthorized beneficiary?
Traditional payment authorization alone cannot answer every one of these questions.
I believe the next generation of fintech platforms will need five critical capabilities:
Agent Identity: Knowing which AI agent is initiating a transaction and on whose behalf.
Verifiable Intent: Establishing exactly what the customer authorized the agent to do.
Dynamic Controls: Enforcing transaction limits, beneficiary restrictions and contextual risk policies.
End-to-End Traceability: Maintaining auditable evidence of decisions, approvals and execution.
Accountability: Defining how exceptions, disputes and unauthorized actions are handled.

This goes beyond adding AI capabilities to existing payment systems.
It represents a shift from transaction-centric authorization to intent-aware financial infrastructure.

The next big fintech opportunity may not be about moving money faster.
It may be about making autonomous money movement trustworthy.

Here's a question for fintech architects and technology leaders:
Are our current payment platforms architecturally prepared for AI agents to become active participants in financial transactions, or are we underestimating the transformation required?

You explain your business.

You convince one investor.

💰 $1 MILLION FOR 30% EQUITY.
ㅤ
Five Sharks.
ㅤ
One entrepreneur.
ㅤ
One extraordinary investment moment.
ㅤ
But here's where the story becomes a powerful business lesson.
ㅤ
In 2017, the Federal Trade Commission challenged Breathometer's advertising claims about the accuracy of its breathalyzer devices.
ㅤ
The company agreed to a settlement without admitting wrongdoing.
ㅤ
And the story became a reminder that even an impressive investment deal cannot guarantee business success.
ㅤ
Because winning investors and winning customers are two completely different things.
ㅤ
💡 5 LESSONS EVERY ENTREPRENEUR SHOULD LEARN FROM THIS DEAL.
ㅤ
→ 🎯 1. Investor excitement is not product validation.
ㅤ
Getting funding means investors believe there is an opportunity.
ㅤ
It doesn't automatically prove that the product performs as promised.
ㅤ
→ 📊 2. Evidence matters more than presentation.
ㅤ
A compelling pitch can open doors.
ㅤ
But reliable testing, accurate claims, and real customer results are what build credibility.
ㅤ
→ 🧠 3. Due diligence protects everyone.
ㅤ
Before investing, evaluate the technology, financials, regulatory requirements, and operational risks.
ㅤ
Enthusiasm should never replace investigation.
ㅤ
→ 🤝 4. A famous investor cannot fix every business problem.
ㅤ
Connections, mentorship, and capital can accelerate growth.
ㅤ
But the product still needs to deliver genuine value.
ㅤ
→ 🚀 5. Sustainable success requires accountability.
ㅤ
When a company makes a promise, customers expect that promise to be fulfilled.
ㅤ
Trust is difficult to earn and easy to lose.
ㅤ
🔥 HERE'S THE BIGGER LEADERSHIP LESSON.

Entrepreneurs often celebrate the wrong milestones.
ㅤ
They celebrate raising millions.
ㅤ
They celebrate appearing on television.
ㅤ
They celebrate impressive valuations.
ㅤ
They celebrate attracting influential investors.
ㅤ
And those achievements can be meaningful.
ㅤ
But none of them replaces the fundamentals.
ㅤ
Does your product work?
ㅤ
Does it solve a real problem?
ㅤ
Can customers trust your promises?
ㅤ
Can your business grow responsibly?
ㅤ
These are the questions that matter long after the cameras stop recording.

💯 REMEMBER THIS.
ㅤ
Funding creates opportunity.
ㅤ
Marketing creates attention.
ㅤ
A strong network creates connections.

Over the years, I’ve been fortunate to lead, mentor, and learn alongside some incredible people.

Recently, a few of those individuals encouraged me to start capturing and sharing some of the leadership lessons I’ve learned along the way.

I’ve been thinking about where to share those reflections, and I figured LinkedIn might be a good place to start.

I don’t know exactly what this will become, or how often I’ll share, but my hope is simple: that something I’ve learned through my own experiences, successes, and mistakes might resonate with someone else navigating their leadership journey.

And perhaps, through the perspectives and experiences of others, I’ll continue learning along the way.

So, here goes…

Leadership Lesson #1  |  Trust Is a Performance Multiplier

We often think of trust as something we build to strengthen relationships.

But trust does something else that is equally powerful: it accelerates performance.

When people feel trusted, they take ownership, they challenge assumptions, they share ideas, and move with greater confidence.

The intersection of trust and accountability is where extraordinary teams are built.  Trust your teams to perform and then measurement shows them that their progress is seen and appreciated.  

The question isn’t simply whether your team trusts you. It’s whether your leadership gives them the confidence to trust themselves.

Most B2B campaigns don't have a content problem. They have a buyer-understanding problem.
We spend time deciding which channels to use, what formats to publish, and how frequently to post.

But sometimes, we miss a more important question:
What problem is our buyer actually trying to solve?

Before planning a B2B campaign, I would map five things.
1. The Trigger
What has changed in the buyer's business that makes this problem important now?
2. The Job to Be Done
What outcome is the buyer trying to achieve, beyond simply purchasing a product or service?
3. The Objection
What could prevent them from moving forward? Cost, complexity, implementation risk, or uncertainty?
4. The Evidence
What would make our proposed solution credible? Relevant experience, case studies, technical proof, or measurable outcomes?
5. The Next Action
What is the most useful next step in their decision-making journey?

These five elements create what I call a B2B Buyer Problem Canvas.
They help connect buyer research with positioning, content, and campaign execution.

Because effective B2B marketing isn't just about communicating what a company offers.
It's about demonstrating why that offering matters to the right buyer, at the right moment.

Your B2B marketing strategy comes down to two questions.

Most companies answer neither, then wonder why the messaging isn’t landing.

Question 1: Is your product necessary?

Necessary = mission critical. Payroll, security, accounting etc

Non-necessary = nice to have. AI automation tools, marketing agencies (guilty)

Question 2: Does the buyer already know who you are?

That gives you four groups.

Group 1 - Necessary product, known company.

Approach: Safety - target the majority with the repeated message you are the choice that is the most likely to allow them to keep their job.

Group 2 - Necessary product, unknown company.

Approach: Upside - target early adopters & innovators with calculated risks that the upside of choosing your brand is exponentially larger than the risks. 

Group 3 - Non-necessary product, known company.

Approach: Belief - educate on why this matters and who else is already doing it. Social proof plus a bit of FOMO, this should get the new line-item signed off. 

Group 4 - Non-necessary product, unknown company.

Approach: Conviction - the old way is dying, here’s why, and here’s the personal pain that made me build this - the founder’s story is the proof.

If I had to start my 2027 B2B marketing strategy today, these would be my first 5 moves:

1. Look back at 2026 and figure out what actually produced pipeline.

2. Decide who you’re going after in 2027, and who you’re not.

3. Define what a good 2027 looks like.

4. Talk to your customers about their goals for 2027.

5. Walk into the budget conversation with that plan in your hands.

That last point is the reason I’d start now and not in January. At most companies I work with, next year’s marketing budget gets decided in November or December. Finance takes last year’s spend, cuts a percentage, and in January marketing hears the number.

The strategy then turns into a way to split that number over the same channels as last year, whether they worked or not.

If you show up with a plan before that number is fixed, you can argue for the budget your plan needs. If you show up after, you’re building a plan around money that’s already been divided.

There’s a second reason. Demand gen is slow. Around 97% of your market isn’t buying right now, so what you start in Q1 mostly pays off in Q3 or later. Every month you spend planning in the new year is a month you’ll feel in your pipeline in the autumn.

So start before the holidays. Even a rough plan is enough to bring to the budget conversation, and that conversation is happening now.

A product can be useful and still be incredibly difficult to sell.

I’ve seen this distinction get overlooked in marketing conversations.

Think about the difference between buying something because it’s nice to have and buying something because you genuinely need it to solve a problem.

That’s the thinking behind the “Sell Painkillers, Not Vitamins” framework in the visual.

And it becomes particularly interesting when you look at B2C versus B2B.

In B2C, an immediate personal need, convenience or aspiration can often trigger a purchase. The customer sees the value and can make the decision independently.

In B2B, the same urgency can exist, but the buying journey is more complicated.

A business might desperately need a solution, but the decision could involve budgets, multiple stakeholders, internal approvals and a clear expectation of ROI.

For example, a productivity tool might sound useful to a team. But if it doesn’t solve a pressing operational problem or demonstrate measurable value, it can remain on the “maybe someday” list.

On the other hand, if the same tool helps reduce costly delays, eliminate repetitive work or prevent revenue leakage, the conversation changes.

The product hasn’t necessarily changed. The problem it solves has become more important to the buyer.

That’s a distinction worth thinking about when building your positioning and GTM strategy.

Don’t just communicate what your product does. Understand what makes someone need it, why they need it now, and what makes the purchase worth prioritising.

Because being useful gets you noticed. Being relevant to an urgent problem gives people a reason to act.

THE BRUTAL TRUTH ABOUT VENTURE CAPITALISTS.

When I started investing nearly 40 years ago, we were called Vulture Capitalists. Frankly, some deserved the name.

But here’s something many Founders don’t understand.

VCs are fundraisers too.

They raise money from pension funds, institutions, family offices and wealthy individuals. Then invest it in businesses like yours. And they’re under enormous pressure to deliver returns.

But here’s the catch.

A perfectly good business can be a TERRIBLE VC investment.

Imagine building a company with £5m in revenue, £1m in profit and 50 employees.

Jobs created. Customers delighted. A sustainable business. Surely a success?

Not necessarily to a VC.

A typical VC fund runs for around 10 years. Its investors expect their capital back, plus substantial returns.

And because many investments won’t deliver, a handful of winners must make up the difference.

There’s a rule of thumb in venture capital: one or two investments need to “return the fund”.

For a $50m fund, that could mean one or two investments generating $50m in proceeds between them. For a $1bn fund, the ambition scales accordingly.

Sometimes that demands returns of 20, 30 or even 40 times the original investment.

So VCs aren’t simply looking for successful businesses. They’re looking for EXTRAORDINARY investment returns. Within a timeframe that suits their fund.

And that’s where things get interesting.

The Founder wants to build a business. The VC wants to generate an investment return.

Those ambitions can align beautifully. But they’re not necessarily the same thing.

A Founder might be delighted to build a profitable £20m business over 15 years. A VC might need it to be worth £200m in seven.

Same business. Same shareholders. COMPLETELY different definitions of success.

And here’s another uncomfortable truth.

VCs have businesses to run too. Management fees pay salaries. Successful exits help raise the next fund.

Without another fund, the investment firm itself may have no future.

So when a VC pushes you to grow faster, raise more money or pursue a bigger exit, ask: Is that best for MY business? Or THEIR fund?

Sometimes both. Sometimes not.

That’s why choosing an investor is like choosing a life partner. Once you’ve taken their money, you’re effectively married. And divorce can be extraordinarily expensive.

I’m not saying VCs are villains. I’ve spent most of my working life being one. Venture capital can be an extraordinary force for innovation.

But it’s not right for every business. And not every Founder should want it.

The biggest mistake isn’t taking VC money. It’s taking it without understanding what your investor needs from you.

So, Founders, before you accept a VC’s money, ask:

“What does success look like for YOUR fund, and is that compatible with what success looks like for ME?”

Because if you don’t agree on the destination, it’s going to be a very difficult marriage.

In venture capital, you don't need every bet to win.

You need one bet to win big.

One of the most interesting concepts I came across in the book 'A Billion Bets' by Aviral Bhatnagar is the asymmetric nature of venture building.

Traditional lenders, such as banks, look for predictable cash flows, repayment capacity and security before lending.

Venture capital operates differently.

VCs invest in businesses that may have little revenue, unproven business models and uncertain outcomes. They accept a high probability of failure in exchange for the possibility of extraordinary returns.

This brings us to an important concept: The Power Law.

In venture capital, returns are rarely distributed evenly.

A small number of investments can generate the majority of a fund's returns, sometimes compensating for losses across several other investments.

There are a few business lessons here:
1. Risk and return are not always symmetrical - A failed investment can cost a VC its invested capital. But a successful breakout company can deliver multiples of that investment.

2. Portfolio thinking matters - VCs don't evaluate every investment in isolation. They build portfolios knowing that a few exceptional winners can drive overall returns.

3. Scale changes the equation - Venture capital looks for businesses with the potential to grow disproportionately. The objective is not simply to build a profitable company, but to back one that can create outsized value.

Takeaway?

Traditional finance often asks "How certain is the repayment?". Venture capital asks "How large can the opportunity become?".

Thoroughly enjoyed reading A Billion Bets. Thank you, Aviral Bhatnagar, for putting together such an insightful compilation and making concepts like asymmetric returns and the power law easier to appreciate.

Venture capital assumes most of its investments will fail. Philanthropy, in my experience, often funds as if every grant has to succeed.

I made that point on a panel in Singapore earlier this month, and it resurfaced when I read Gabrielle Fitzgerald's piece on “third wave philanthropy” yesterday (link below). Estimates suggest the #AI IPOs could create up to $450 billion in new philanthropic capital, much of it guided by the #EffectiveAltruism language of cost-effectiveness and counterfactuals. Gabrielle’s closing question is how to balance the drive for rapid, cost-effective results with the sustained investment that lasting impact requires. Two points from my panel, Capital for Impact: Where Venture Capital Meets Venture Philanthropy, at the Business & Philanthropy Forum, speak to this.

1️⃣ The first is to decide at the outset who will pay for the work in the long run, because that tells you how patient the funding needs to be. For neglected tropical diseases, donated medicines make treatment one of the best buys in global health, but results only last once governments take on the cost of delivery, which builds over years, often starting with a single budget line. Making paediatric antiretrovirals affordable was different: at CHAI, my team helped several African governments pool reliable orders, increasing manufacturers’ trust in the demand and enabling lower prices and a more sustainable market. Rapid, cost-effective results and lasting impact are compatible when funding is built around who will own the work, rather than a parallel system that depends on the next grant.

2️⃣ Second, venture and impact capital each hold half the measurement answer. Venture capital has a precise scorecard that measures financial return; impact capital has the right goal but too often counts outputs rather than outcomes. They can converge around:

💰 Cost per outcome, the closest thing philanthropy has to unit economics, and what effective altruists call cost-effectiveness.

🔮 Leading indicators: with deworming, we could count treatments within weeks, but the effects on schooling and earnings took years to show. Tracking earlier signals, such as treatment coverage or a government’s first budget line for delivery, lets funders back the next stage without waiting a decade for verified, long-term outcomes.

The new wealth Gabrielle describes can fund both speed and sustainability, if it is informed from the start by who will carry the work forward.

My thanks to Fabien A. of the Pan-African Council for moderating, to my fellow panelists Kotaro Tamura, Dr. Viveka Kalidasan, PhD, and Martin O'Dee, and to John Wei Zheng and the ALLIANCE FOR GOOD team.
