FROM SALES EXECUTIVE TO STRATEGIC BUSINESS PARTNER: CREATING VALUE BEYOND THE SALE 

In B2B sales, there is a significant difference between simply selling a product or service and becoming a strategic partner to your customers.

A transactional approach focuses mainly on closing the next deal.

A strategic approach focuses on understanding the customer’s business, identifying opportunities and contributing to their long-term success.

I believe this evolution requires four key principles:

 1. UNDERSTAND THE CUSTOMER’S BUSINESS

Go beyond the product or service you sell. Understand your customer’s strategy, challenges, market position and business objectives.

 2. CREATE SOLUTIONS, NOT JUST OFFERS

Connect your products or services to real business needs. Bring ideas, alternatives and solutions that generate measurable value.

 3. BUILD A TRUST-BASED PARTNERSHIP

Be consistent, transparent and reliable. Share knowledge, communicate proactively and demonstrate that your interest goes beyond the immediate transaction.

 4. THINK ABOUT LONG-TERM GROWTH

Identify new opportunities, anticipate future needs and help your customers evolve. Sustainable business growth should create value for both sides.

In International B2B Sales, this mindset is particularly important. Different markets, cultures and business environments require adaptability, knowledge and a long-term perspective.

The strongest commercial relationships are not built around a single transaction. They are built around shared objectives and mutual success.

The best sales professionals don’t just sell to their customers. They become partners in their growth.

قسمت دوم: فروش سازمانی (B2B Sales)

فروش سازمانی چیست؟

فروش سازمانی (Business to Business) به فرآیندی گفته می‌شود که در آن یک شرکت، محصولات یا خدمات خود را به شرکت یا سازمان دیگری عرضه می‌کند.

در این مدل فروش، برخلاف فروش مستقیم به مصرف‌کننده نهایی، تصمیم‌گیری معمولاً توسط چند نفر از مدیران یا افراد تأثیرگذار در سازمان انجام می‌شود.

ویژگی‌های اصلی فروش B2B

۱. فرآیند تصمیم‌گیری چندمرحله‌ای: تصمیم خرید معمولاً نیازمند بررسی و تأیید چند واحد سازمانی است.

۲. مذاکره تخصصی: قیمت، شرایط پرداخت، کیفیت و تعهدات تأمین‌کننده اهمیت زیادی دارند.

۳. چرخه فروش طولانی‌تر: تبدیل یک فرصت تجاری به قرارداد ممکن است زمان‌بر باشد.

۴. رابطه بلندمدت: حفظ مشتری و ایجاد همکاری مستمر از اهداف مهم این نوع فروش است.

۵. ارزش قرارداد بالاتر: بسیاری از معاملات سازمانی در حجم و مبالغ قابل‌توجه انجام می‌شوند.

مثال‌هایی از فروش سازمانی

- فروش تجهیزات پزشکی به بیمارستان‌ها و مراکز درمانی
- تأمین مواد اولیه کارخانه‌ها
- فروش محصولات غذایی به هتل‌ها و رستوران‌ها
- ارائه نرم‌افزارهای سازمانی به شرکت‌ها

چه چیزی فروش B2B را موفق می‌کند؟

شناخت دقیق کسب‌وکار مشتری، توانایی مذاکره، ارائه راهکار متناسب با نیاز سازمان و ایجاد اعتماد بلندمدت.

در فروش سازمانی، هدف فقط فروش یک محصول نیست؛ بلکه ایجاد یک رابطه تجاری پایدار و سودآور است.

“Be more strategic” is feedback in a trench coat. Underneath, it’s 1 of 3 complaints all dressed up.

 💸 “I can’t see how this connects to revenue.”
Translation: your updates read like an activity log. Posts, opens, events, more posts. Lead with the business goal, then the 1 or 2 things marketing did to move it.

 🎯 “I don’t know what you’d stop doing.”
Translation: you said yes to everything, so nothing looks like a priority. Name what you’re not doing this quarter, and why. In writing.

 😠 “I’m hearing about problems from sales before I hear them from you.”
Translation: bad news is traveling faster than you are. Bring it first, with a fix attached.

Can’t tell which one you got? Ask: “Can you give me an example of something I did that felt strategic, and something that didn’t?”

Then watch them think about it. Most CEOs can answer. And once you know which complaint it was, the fix is a lot smaller than the feedback made it sound.

Before next year's budget is finalized, examine these two numbers:

The percentage of bookings coming from your current customers.
The share of your marketing spend dedicated to growing those accounts. 

For most B2B companies, there will be a huge gap between these two figures.
Most B2B businesses see large shares of their bookings come from upsells and cross-sells, driven by deeper relationships with current customers. 

But most dollars spent on marketing still go toward pursuing new logos. 

Why? 

Because it is easy for marketing leaders to measure new-logo pipeline. It is also easy for them to communicate this success to the C-Suite and/or board. 

So after a deal closes, that customer account is frequently transferred over to the responsible customer success team. 

Marketing is no longer measured on what happens next: adoption, retention, cross-sells, or upsells. So the budget naturally follows the metrics marketing is held accountable for.

This results in two expensive blind spots:

The part of the business producing some of the most consistent growth gets little support from marketing.

Marketing receives little or no credit when it contributes to expansion revenue.

No one is saying spend should match bookings dollar for dollar. Winning a new customer will always cost more than growing an existing one.

But if your budget is wildly out of proportion to where your revenue actually comes from, it may be time to add an expansion metric to marketing’s scorecard.

Posting once a week and wondering why nobody sees you is like turning your shop lights on one day a month.

In B2B and B2C marketing alike, sporadic visibility destroys momentum.

• Algorithms favor habitual creators
• Audiences require repeated touchpoints to build trust
• Inconsistency communicates a lack of reliability

Are you showing up daily for your target audience, or are you keeping your business in the dark?

SA Venture Capital and Private Equity Association (SAVCA)’s 2026 Venture Capital Industry Survey (2025 calendar year) shows capital concentrating:

👉 R2.48bn allocated across 212 deals, versus 222 in 2024
👉 Those deals reached 91 companies, down from 110
👉 Average of 2.3 rounds per funded company

Managers are reserving for and supporting existing positions rather than widening the portfolio. For LPs, that makes reserve strategy and follow-on discipline central to manager selection.

The exits are where this survey earns its weight. Ten exits were reported in 2025, six of them profitable. Those six returned R281.2m on R99.3m invested, roughly 2.8x. That multiple covers the profitable exits only. It is not a cohort-wide return, and ten exits is too small a sample to treat as a trend. But after a long wait for realisations in this market, it is a data point LPs should note.

Three questions we would put to any manager in this environment:
1. What governs the decision to reinvest, and how is that separated from the original investment case?
2. Is the route to exit defined at entry, or assumed at exit?
3. How much of reported performance has been returned to LPs?

These questions apply across private capital in South Africa. At RH Managers, they shape how we have invested in healthcare infrastructure for 12 years, through a financial, operational and ESG due diligence framework applied before capital is committed.

Concentration without rigour compounds risk, with it, compounds returns.

A distribution center reports 98% productivity. AI analyzes the numbers and recommends reducing staffing.
But what if the productivity calculation excludes overtime, temporary workers, or quality failures?
AI might produce a perfectly logical recommendation based on fundamentally misleading data.
The danger: A sophisticated analysis can make bad information look credible.

65% of UK businesses that have not adopted AI say they have no clear business case for it.

That is a bigger barrier than the technology itself.

The UK government's latest AI survey shows business AI adoption doubled from 16% to 32% in just 12 months. And half of businesses already using AI reported productivity gains.

But there is a gap between knowing AI matters and knowing exactly where it creates value.

At IIH Global, every client conversation starts with one question: What specific business outcome are you trying to change?

Because successful AI adoption starts with a business problem, not a technology.

Interesting UNSW Business School podcast episode with ESCoE Leadership Executive member Kevin Fox on AI and how we can measure its impact on productivity.

“Most organizations are trying to scale AI. The most successful CAIOs are scaling a new way of working. Then AI follows.”

What a wonderful quote.

IBM has just published fabulous research, conducted in partnership with Oxford Economics, involving 1,667 senior AI executives across 20 industries and 33 geographies.

They identified eight management and organisational behaviours that together explain nearly 80% of the observed variation in enterprise AI success in their statistical model.

These include embedding AI directly into workflows, enabling AI to act autonomously, retaining the ability to intervene, redesigning business models, reallocating resources based on evidence and reinvesting productivity gains.

The more successful organisations aren't just better at implementing AI. They're better at organising around it.

My entire book is premised on that. Great feeling.

And there's a lovely paradox in the research. Whilst 96% of high-impact Chief AI Officers report that AI-generated outputs can trigger autonomous actions, compared with 40% of the others, they're also nearly four times as likely to be able to pause, adjust or redirect their AI systems without disrupting operations.

Greater autonomy AND greater control.

I met Philippe Gralll at Thinkers50 in London. 

He’s an executive coach to CEOs across industries including luxury, retail and pharma, and we’re both in Marshall Goldsmith’s #100Coaches community. 

So, I invited him to talk to my class about working in the age of AI.

Underneath:

 👉 Mindset: your why, the part AI can’t replace

 👉 System: how you structure, teach and operate your AI

 👉 Technology: one brain, specialist hands
 
The leadership lessons I took from it:

 🔷 Stay curious. The leaders who win ask “what if?” before “what’s the risk?”

 🔷 Learn by doing. You can’t read your way into AI fluency.

 🔷 Start small. Run a pilot, not a transformation program.

 🔷 Fail fast. Trial and error is the strategy, not the detour.

 🔷 Share your learning. Every experiment teaches more when others see it.

 🔷 Stay open-minded. The best use case may not be the one you planned.
 
The students got it. They didn’t ask which tool to buy. They asked what to hand over, what to keep, where to start, and how to keep learning. That’s the right instinct.

🔥🔆Leadership 2.0: Why Great Leadership Starts with Emotional Intelligence🔆🔥

In today's fast-changing workplace, technical expertise and professional experience are important, but they are not enough to make someone an effective leader.

Great leadership requires more than managing tasks and delivering results. It requires the ability to adapt to change, understand people, manage emotions, and inspire others.

This is one of my key takeaways from Leadership 2.0 by Travis Bradberry and Jean Greaves, authors of Emotional Intelligence 2.0.

The book highlights the importance of combining Adaptive Leadership with Emotional Intelligence (EQ) to become a more effective leader.

Here are five lessons that particularly stood out to me:

1️⃣ Adaptive Leadership

Great leaders don't resist change, they embrace it. They remain flexible, open to learning, and capable of guiding their teams through uncertainty.

2️⃣ Self-Awareness

Effective leadership starts with knowing yourself. Understanding your emotions, strengths, weaknesses, and how your behavior affects others is essential.

3️⃣ Self-Management

Knowing how you feel is one thing, managing how you respond is another. Great leaders remain composed under pressure, manage stress, and avoid impulsive reactions.

4️⃣ Social Awareness

Leadership is about people. It requires listening actively, showing empathy, understanding different perspectives, and recognizing the needs of others.

5️⃣ Relationship Management

This is where emotional intelligence translates into leadership impact. Building trust, managing conflicts, developing people, and creating positive relationships are essential to leading successful teams.

My Biggest Takeaway 💡

Leadership is not about a title or position. It is a continuous journey of self-awareness, learning, and adaptation.

The best leaders are not necessarily those who have all the answers, but those who understand themselves, connect with others, and bring out the best in their teams.

‼️Ultimately, before you can effectively lead others, you must first learn to lead yourself.

Stop Trying to Book the Meeting. Start Earning It.

I came across a sales training post this morning outlining five discovery questions designed to help salespeople book more meetings.

Good questions, actually.

Understand the customer’s situation. Identify their problems. Explore the implications. Then ask for the meeting.

Nothing fundamentally wrong with that approach.

But I think we’re missing something important.

The objective of discovery shouldn’t be to book a meeting. It should be to determine whether there’s a good reason to have one.

Those are two very different things.

Over the years, I’ve watched salespeople become so focused on advancing an opportunity that they forget to establish whether an opportunity actually exists.

They ask questions designed to uncover pain.

And when the customer says everything is working fine, they keep digging.

Surely something must be wrong.

Surely there’s a problem hiding somewhere.

Surely if we ask the right question, we’ll find something we can sell them.

Maybe.

Or maybe the customer is telling you the truth.

Here’s a concept that shouldn’t be revolutionary.

Not everyone needs what you’re selling.

And that’s perfectly fine.

One of the most valuable skills a salesperson can develop is recognizing the difference between a customer who has a problem worth solving and someone who simply agreed to answer a few questions.

I’ve spent much of my career in complex sales environments, including enterprise technology, where relationships and credibility often matter considerably more than the immediate transaction.

And I’ve learned something.

Sometimes the most productive sales conversation ends with you telling the customer that you don’t think they need your product.

Imagine that.

A salesperson who actually recommends against making a purchase.

You might lose a transaction.

But you could gain something considerably more valuable.

Trust.

And trust has a funny way of generating opportunities that no discovery script could ever anticipate.

Now, don’t misunderstand me.

I believe in disciplined sales processes. I believe in asking thoughtful questions. And I absolutely believe in understanding the financial and operational implications of a customer’s challenges.

But there’s a difference between genuine curiosity and a rehearsed interrogation designed to manufacture urgency.

Customers can usually tell which one they’re experiencing.

The best salespeople don’t just know when to ask for the meeting. They know when not to.

Because the objective isn’t to fill your calendar.

It’s to build relationships that eventually fill your pipeline.

And there’s a world of difference.

Here’s my question for sales leaders: Are we teaching our teams how to discover opportunities, or simply how to manufacture appointments?

#TheAccidentalInnovator #SalesLeadership #ConsultativeSelling #SalesStrategy #ExecutiveLeadership #B2BSales #CustomerRelationships #BusinessDevelopment

Sales teams have more technology, more data and more automation than ever before.

Yet one question deserves more attention: are we actually improving the quality of our customer conversations?

AI can research prospects, identify buying signals, prepare follow-ups and reduce administrative work. But it cannot replace a salesperson's ability to understand a customer's real challenge, ask the right questions and build confidence in a decision.

That is where the real opportunity lies.

The strongest sales teams will not use AI simply to increase the number of activities they complete. They will use it to make every interaction more relevant, informed and valuable.

Technology should create more room for meaningful conversations, not more noise.

The future of sales belongs to teams that combine intelligent systems with better human judgment.

Know when to cut your losses. Recognize when something isn’t working and it’s time to change direction.

Know your value and make the ask. Be clear about what you’re building, what you bring, and what you need. Can you explain it in 30 to 60 seconds?

I’m excited to share some of the business books I’ve read so far 📚. Each book has given me a new perspective on business and personal growth, and I’d like to share some of the core lessons that have stuck with me from each one.

The Lean Startup by Eric Ries: This book taught me that you don't need to have everything figured out before starting. Testing an MVP can save you time and money on ideas that might not work. The core principle is simple: build, measure, and learn.

The $100 Startup by Chris Guillebeau: The idea I loved most from this book is that you don't need a huge budget to start a business. This book provides a framework for building a business focused on creating value and solving real problems.

The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss: Being busy can be a form of laziness. Staying occupied doesn't always mean being productive. By eliminating or delegating unnecessary tasks and focusing on your Most Important Tasks (MITs), you can achieve much more.

The Personal MBA by Josh Kaufman: A book that covers key aspects of business, including value creation, finance, sales, marketing, value delivery, psychology, leadership, and much more. It offers practical ideas that challenge the way you think about business.

This Is Marketing by Seth Godin: The key idea I took away is that marketing isn't just about selling; it's about understanding people and creating something that genuinely matters to them.

How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie: This was one of the first books I read. One lesson that stuck with me is that listening, understanding others, and showing genuine interest can be far more powerful than simply trying to convince them.

We Have a Deal by Natalie Reynolds: This book taught me to approach negotiation differently, recognize common negotiation mistakes, ask better questions, and handle objections effectively.

I'm still learning, and there's a lot more to read. Every book on this list has been worth my time. One thing I've realized is that reading is only the first step. The real value comes from applying what you learn.

YOU CANNOT DEMAND EXCEPTIONAL SALES RESULTS FROM A TEAM YOU HAVE NOT INVESTED IN DEVELOPING.

Targets don't train people. Pressure doesn't build competence. And constant supervision does not automatically create high performers.

Yet, many organisations continue to raise sales targets without giving equal attention to the training, mentoring and empowerment of the people expected to achieve them.

THE IMPORTANCE OF TRAINING, MENTORING AND EMPOWERING SALES TEAMS
One of the most valuable lessons I have learned throughout my experience in sales and team leadership is that sustainable performance begins with people development.

A successful sales team is not built by setting ambitious targets alone. It is built by developing the skills, confidence, motivation and capabilities of team members.
Effective sales leadership requires:
✅ Training: Equip team members with the product knowledge, selling techniques, communication skills and objection-handling abilities needed to succeed.
✅ Mentoring: Provide continuous guidance, constructive feedback and practical support to help team members overcome challenges and grow professionally.
✅ Empowerment: Give employees the confidence, responsibility and opportunity to make decisions, take initiative and contribute meaningfully.
✅ Motivation: Recognise effort, celebrate achievements and create an environment where employees feel valued.
✅ Accountability: Establish clear expectations, monitor performance fairly and encourage ownership of individual and team results.

Throughout my experience recruiting, training and supervising sales professionals, I have come to understand that leadership is not simply about achieving results through people. It is also about developing people who can consistently deliver results.
When organisations invest in their sales teams, they build more than a productive workforce. They develop confident professionals, strengthen customer relationships, improve employee commitment and create a foundation for sustainable business growth.
Great leaders do not simply demand performance. They develop the people who make performance possible.

💬 As a leader or sales professional, which do you believe has the greatest impact on sales performance: training, mentoring, motivation or empowerment?

After 15 years of building RecruitMe Plus, the best sales strategy I've ever used is one I'll never change.

HONESTY

I've read about sales techniques
Negotiation tactics
Buyer psychology
How to identify pain points
How to create urgency
How to handle objections
Some people even recommend bluffing

But the strategy that's worked best for me has always been much simpler:
Tell the truth!

If we can deliver something, I say we can
If we can't, I say we can't

If a client's expectations are unrealistic, I tell them

If the salary won't attract the talent they want, I tell them

If I don't believe we can successfully close a search, I'd rather walk away than sell a promise my team can't keep

Does that mean I win every deal?
Of course not.

I've probably lost business because of it.

But I've also built client relationships that lasted for years!

Because once expectations are clearly set, something important happens:
Trust replaces selling
You don't need to constantly manage disappointment
You don't need to explain promises you shouldn't have made
You don't need to remember what you told someone during the sales process

You simply deliver what you said you would.

After 15 years, I've learned that the best sales strategy isn't always the cleverest one

Sometimes it's simply:
Never sell something you don't believe you can deliver.

It may cost you a deal today, but trust me, it can win you a client for years.

🚀 7 STRATEGIES TO EXPAND YOUR BUSINESS INTO NEW MARKETS

Business growth isn't just about selling more products or services. It's about identifying new opportunities, reaching the right customers, building strong relationships, and expanding your market presence.

If you're planning to take your business to the next level, here are 7 powerful strategies to successfully enter new markets.

1️⃣ Conduct In-Depth Market Research
Understand your target audience, customer behavior, market demand, competitors, industry trends, and potential business opportunities before entering a new market.

2️⃣ Identify the Right Target Audience
Define your ideal customer profile (ICP). Understand customer pain points, purchasing behavior, demographics, and expectations to build an effective customer acquisition strategy.

3️⃣ Develop a Strong Market Entry Strategy
Choose the right approach, whether it's direct sales, strategic partnerships, franchising, distribution networks, or digital expansion.

4️⃣ Build Strategic Business Partnerships
Connect with local businesses, distributors, industry experts, and potential partners. Strong business relationships can accelerate market penetration and brand awareness.

5️⃣ Adapt Your Products and Marketing Strategy
Every market is different. Customize your products, pricing strategy, branding, and marketing campaigns according to local customer needs and market preferences.

6️⃣ Leverage Digital Marketing and Technology
Use SEO, content marketing, social media marketing, LinkedIn marketing, email marketing, and targeted advertising to increase brand visibility and generate qualified leads.

7️⃣ Monitor Performance and Scale Strategically
Track KPIs such as customer acquisition cost (CAC), conversion rates, revenue growth, customer retention, and market share. Analyze results and continuously optimize your business growth strategy.

💡 Remember: Successful market expansion doesn't happen overnight. It requires proper planning, market intelligence, customer understanding, consistent execution, and long-term relationship building.

More traffic! More clicks! More ad spend! If it continues, your website might need a bigger door just to let everyone in. 😅

My unpopular opinion: more visitors don't automatically mean more revenue.
Before spending more to bring people in, you should think: How much more could your business earn from the traffic you're already paying for?

That's where Conversion Rate Optimization (CRO) becomes an important part of the growth strategy.

CRO isn't just about increasing the percentage of visitors who buy, but about identifying friction across the customer journey, running experiments, and measuring whether those changes greatly improve business outcomes.

For example, take our work with Karma & Luck:

We identified opportunities across three areas:
→ Product discovery: Helping customers find products more easily.
→ Site speed: Addressing friction that could interrupt the shopping experience.
→ Bundle purchasing: Improving the experience to encourage bigger baskets.

After experimentation, the results were significant:
📈 Conversion rate: 1.20% → 1.95% (+62.5%)
🛒 Average order value: $120 → $170 (+41.7%)
💰 Revenue per visitor: $1.44 → $3.32 (+130%)

Now, consider what that could mean at scale.

With 100,000 visitors, the presentation models revenue increasing from $144,000 to $331,500 - an additional $187,500 without increasing traffic.

That's the potential of improving both how many visitors convert and how much they spend.
The opportunity isn't limited to e-commerce. A SaaS business might focus on trial-to-paid conversion or qualified pipeline. A travel company might optimize completed bookings and booking revenue. The right metrics depend on the business model and its goals.

More acquisition can help you grow, but testing, learning from customer behavior, and implementing winning experiments can help you get more value from the demand you've already created.

Asking out of curiosity, what do you think is the bigger growth mistake: not investing enough in customer acquisition, or scaling acquisition before your website is ready to convert?

Find a challenge people face repeatedly—not just an idea that sounds exciting.

2️⃣ Understand Your Users
Know who experiences the problem, how they solve it today, and what's missing.

3️⃣ Validate Before You Build
Talk to potential customers. Test your assumptions. Make sure people actually need your solution.

4️⃣ Build Around the Problem
Start with the core functionality that solves the biggest pain point. Add features as users grow.

Think about it:
Problem → User Research → MVP → Feedback → Scalable SaaS Product.

The best SaaS products aren't necessarily the ones with the most features.

They're the ones that solve a problem so well that customers don't want to go back to their old way of working.

• MERCOSUR: Regional economic and trade integration.
• Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN): Financial technology collaboration.
• Nexus Global Payments: Cross-border instant payment connectivity.

AI-driven banking, open finance, digital identity, tokenisation, CBDCs, stablecoins, cybersecurity, AML/CFT and data governance are shaping the next phase.

THE BIGGER PICTURE →

Fragmented infrastructure, currency differences, remittance costs and regulatory divergence make regional interoperability a strategic priority.

Connecting national payment systems and financial institutions could unlock a more integrated regional ecosystem.

The next frontier is regional financial intelligence and connectivity.

The future of payments isn't a choice between traditional banking and new technology.
I think it's increasingly clear that we'll need both.

Yesterday, U.S. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller made an important point about digital finance: new payment technologies will continue to develop, but established financial infrastructure and central bank money will remain essential to trust. That distinction matters.

There's a tendency in fintech to frame innovation as replacing whatever came before it. Banks versus fintechs. Traditional payment networks versus blockchain. Old infrastructure versus new. But financial systems rarely evolve that neatly. The real opportunity is to connect these technologies in ways that improve how money moves without compromising reliability, oversight or customer confidence.

For me, the most interesting companies won't necessarily be those trying to replace the entire financial system. They'll be the ones making its different parts work better together.

Nice to see Clariteer in Trends, De Tijd and La Libre today 😊
 
People often ask me why I started another company after Proxyclick. Part of the answer is simple: it’s a fascinating problem, and I’m lucky to work on it with Gregory Blondeau, Caroline Deuse and Jan-Pieter George. But there’s another reason, and it goes back to my first VC investment.
 
After the sale, I invested into a climate fund through Carbon Equity. Bill Gates’ book on climate had made a big impression on me. Here in Europe, the climate conversation is mostly about consuming less. Gates shows that innovation is an equally powerful lever, with things like low-carbon steel and cement, and I wanted to be part of that.
 
That’s what I like about venture capital. When you buy an existing share on the stock market, your money goes to whoever sold it to you. In a VC fund, your money goes straight into the companies building the future you want to see.
 
And more people can do this now. Europe is pushing hard to open private equity to individual investors (e.g. ELTIF 2.0), because it sees it as a way to fund its own future next to the US and China.
 
Where it gets painful is ... reporting. Private equity is a sophisticated asset class full of very smart people, yet following your positions still looks like it did decades ago. With listed shares you know exactly where you stand, in real time. With PE funds you receive a steady stream of PDFs, and the one number that matters is often hiding in a footnote on page 37 😅
 
Large institutions have analysts for that. Individual investors and small family offices usually don’t, and end up doing it by hand.
 
That’s what we’re working on at Clariteer: turning that pile of PDFs into one clear, up-to-date view of your portfolio, so you can follow performance, see capital calls coming and handle the tax side. In Belgium, with the new capital gains tax, that last part has become a real headache.
 
Thanks to Trends, De Tijd and La Libre for the coverage 🙏

Close to half of VC decision-makers have backed at least one real winner. Only 3% have backed ten.

Blake Jackson and I have assembled what we believe is the largest and most comprehensive dataset of individual U.S. venture capitalists ever built: over 100,000 professionals affiliated with U.S. VC firms between 1996 and 2025, roughly 37,000 of them investment professionals.

We count an investment as “successful” if the startup subsequently went public, reached a unicorn valuation, or was acquired for at least five times the total capital the company had raised.

45% of middle- and senior-level VCs have at least one successful investment. Roughly a coin flip. If your ambition is to be able to say, at the end of your career, that you backed one real winner, the odds are far better than the folklore suggests. And of course the flip side is just as true: a single hit is not evidence of skill. It is close to the base rate.

Everything changes when you ask not whether a VC ever hit, but how often. Among the decision-makers, 45% reach one, 28% reach two, 11% reach five, and 3% reach ten.

Fewer than four hundred people is the entire population of U.S. venture capitalists over three decades credited with ten or more successful investments. It is smaller than the combined partner rosters of a handful of large firms.

There is no number of wins after which the next one becomes easy. When we randomly reassign VCs across deals, the number of VCs with ten or more successful investments declines substantially. This lends further support to the thesis that skill plays a critical role in long-term VC success.

A few days ago, I shared how I ended up deleting all my AI bots. 😊 The post sparked quite a conversation. So, here's the sequel:

The lesson wasn’t that AI doesn’t work. I was using AI built for flying when I was still crawling.

Every business goes through or is in one of the four stages: Crawl. Walk. Run. Fly. AI can help at every stage & also accelerate the evolution but you need to know which stage you are in.

CRAWL: Get the basics right. Understand your product, market and customers. Use AI for research and positioning.
WALK: Know your customer. Use AI to identify opportunities and prepare meaningful conversations.
RUN: You have traction. Use AI to scale outreach, follow-ups and delivery.
FLY: Your processes are mature. Now automation and AI agents can deliver real scale.

My mistake? Jumping straight to fly.

I had the bots, but not all the foundations to make them effective.

The bigger lesson: 

AI adoption isn’t just a technology decision. It’s a business maturity decision.

Experience and judgement tell you where you are. AI can help you get to the next stage faster.

It’s not about using more or less AI. It’s about creating more value with the right AI at the right time.

- Critical Positions.
- Required Skills & Competencies.
- Hiring Needs.
- Training & Reskilling Opportunities.

- Business as Usual.

- Reporting Lines.

Not every AI use case deserves the same level of governance.

A customer-facing recommendation engine and an internal productivity assistant carry very different risk profiles. 

Treating them identically either slows down low-risk work or under-protects high-risk work.

Before approving an AI use case, consider four dimensions:
Data sensitivity: What type of data is processed?

Business impact: What happens if the system makes a wrong decision?

Autonomy: Is AI supporting a human, or making decisions with limited intervention?
Regulatory exposure: Could the use case trigger privacy, sectoral, employment, consumer or other obligations?

Together, these can help determine whether a use case needs a basic review, an enhanced privacy and security assessment, legal and compliance review, executive approval or ongoing monitoring.

The point is not to create bureaucracy around every AI experiment. It is to apply governance proportionately.

Risk-based governance is usually more sustainable than treating every AI application identically.

Your startup doesn't need more employees. It needs better systems.

Over the years, as an entrepreneur and startup mentor, I have seen founders make one common mistake: whenever operations become overwhelming, their first instinct is to hire more people.

But adding people to an unstructured business often creates more confusion, not efficiency.
Missed follow-ups, delayed decisions, repeated mistakes, unclear responsibilities, and constant founder involvement are not always signs of an understaffed team.

They are often signs of missing systems.

Before expanding your team, focus on building four essential systems:
1. Lead Management System: Track every opportunity, customer interaction, and follow-up.
2. Task & Ownership System: Define who is responsible for what, with clear timelines and accountability.
3. Communication System: Establish structured updates so important information doesn't get lost in endless calls and messages.
4. Reporting System: Use measurable data to identify problems and make better decisions.

A business cannot scale sustainably if every small decision requires the founder's approval.

Your role as a founder should gradually shift from managing every task to building processes, developing leaders, and creating accountability.

Hire people to accelerate growth. Build systems to sustain it.

Because the true strength of a startup is not how many people it employs, but how effectively it operates.

Founders, ask yourself: If you step away for a week, will your business continue running smoothly?

Instead of just accepting it, he started building a solution. That idea became 𝙍𝙚𝙙𝘽𝙪𝙨, now one of India's best-known online bus booking platforms.

Three lessons from the story:

1. 𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐞 𝐚 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐚. Many successful startups begin with a problem the founder faced firsthand. If you keep running into the same friction, someone else probably is too.
2. 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐬𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲. RedBus didn't need a huge budget to begin. It needed a clear problem, a simple product, and enough users to prove the idea worked.

The founder's story is inspiring, but the real takeaway is simpler, 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘆. They're often where the best opportunities are hiding.

FROM CREATIVITY TO INNOVATION: WHAT DOES IT TAKE TO BRING AN IDEA TO MARKET?

On October 22, 2026, I attended the launch of 84X – Unlocking the Path to Market by Van Lang University  and B71. The panel, moderated by Ms. Kylie Lê, left me with six lessons.

1. Innovation starts with a problem, not necessarily a breakthrough idea.

Mr. Vinnie Lauria used Netflix and Blockbuster to show that a more convenient business model can matter more than complex technology.

Looking back at my studies, I often start a project by asking "what product should we make?" and leave the customer for later. Next time, I want to understand who has the problem first.

2. Investors evaluate the people, not only the idea.

As Founding Partner at Golden Gate Ventures, Vinnie looks for:

	•	Vision & Leadership: Can the founder lead a team?
	•	Execution: What have they done, learned, and adjusted?
	•	Scalability: Can the model grow, including internationally?

For students, execution can start small: one talk with a real customer, one simple test, one revision after feedback.

3. Innovation needs a supportive ecosystem.

Mr. Nguyen Duy Vu (CEO, Hanovation) named three resources: education, access to resources, and community support.

It made me rethink networking. Connecting with the right people for the right problem matters more than knowing many people.

4. Triple Helix: Government × Universities × Industry.

Mr. JSERN KHOR stressed clear roles for each party, while Mr. Nguyen Duy Vu suggested bringing real market problems closer to startups. Collaboration creates value when resources are actually connected, not when many organizations simply sign on.

5. Innovation isn't only for people in tech.

Ms. Tuyet Vu  (Managing Partner, Spark Ventures Studio) spoke about the creative economy: design, customer experience, content, and consumer insight.

I used to think innovation had to mean AI or high tech. Now I see that our advantage as students may lie in noticing changes around us and turning them into value.

6. An innovation ecosystem works like a football team.

Jsern (Executive Director, Global Innovation & Impact Center, VLU) compared stakeholders to players in different positions with one goal. If everyone wants to score, who defends?

His question stayed with me: "Who is going to do what and by when?"

It reminded me of group projects in class, where a good plan falls apart when nobody owns a task or a deadline. I want to start every project with that question.

⸻

As a final-year student, I don't want startup knowledge to stay inside presentations and exams. I want to test it in the real world: talk to real people, run small experiments, and fix what doesn't work.

Thank you to the organizers and speakers for such practical perspectives.

Social media is dead...

And that's excellent news if you practice B2B Marketing or if you are simply trying to build your personal brand on LinkedIn. 

In very simple terms, we've gone through three macro phases of social media: 

1.) The golden era of social media (2006 - 2016): Driven by pure network effects with chronological timelines and feeds filled with updates of our connections. 

2.) The Broadcast Media Age (2017 – 2024): A transition phase where feeds started getting separated from connections and where the name of the game was to build a huge following and then broadcast to them (the Kim Kardashian model...) 

3.) The Interest Media Era (2025+): Our feeds are now driven purely by interest and networks or followers mean far less now than they used to. 

In this article I explain why this is GREAT news. Someone with 500 followers and a good content strategy can have the same impact as someone with 50 000 followers.

Deloitte recently published a report on one of the most important topics fintech leaders need to think about when considering implementing AI in their product: Trust
 
Why Trust Is So Important
No matter how good your product is, or how market leading your AI agents are, if you don’t have your user’s trust, they won’t use them. This is true for most products, but even more for money. People have worked incredibly hard for their money and they aren’t about to let you lose it for them
 
Key Themes From The Report
There are various dimensions to the lack of trust in AI (within finance):

1️⃣ Data Sharing Concerns: 72% are concerned about sharing financial information with AI
 
2️⃣ Low Recommendation Trust: only 46% trust the accuracy of AI banking recommendations
 
3️⃣ Financial Action Anxiety: 83% are anxious about AI agents taking financial actions without approving each one
 
But, there are also things people like about AI
4️⃣ Time Savings & Utility: 58% say AI saves time compared to traditional research. 53% say AI gives more useful information than traditional search engines. And 43% say it gives better information than bank websites or apps
 
What This Means for Fintechs and What They Can Do
The good news for fintechs is that trust is not a newly important variable. AI just adds a new dimension as fewer people truly understand how it works. And the bigger the knowledge gap the more care is required:

▷ Uncertainty Aversion: tell people exactly how the AI uses their financial and personal data, and how you are protecting them from any bad outcomes
 
▷ Salience & Transparency: don’t hide anything from users, tell them everything they would want to know. And do it without technical language so they can actually engage with the information
 
▷ Reactance: let people change how much information AI can access and what it’s capable of doing. Give users control
 
Key Takeaways
The value and opportunities for AI are huge, and even customers who are worried about it can admit it. And this puts financial companies in a strong position. Because whether users trust their AI is dependant on their own handling of the communication and user journey
 
If fintechs implement the right communication, framing, and build the right user journeys around it, they can gain users’ trust and increase utilisation

Last Thursday at 1871’s FinTech Innovation Summit, the Chicago Fed showed a slide mapping the technology vendors behind the largest US clearinghouses. There were thousands of them, and a lot of the banks and clearing firms rely on the same few providers.

The same day, I was in a private Corporate Innovation session on that exact topic. Partway through, most of the people in the room stopped receiving email, because they all use Microsoft and it had just gone down.

The outage ended up lasting two days and reached 74 countries. Courts, banks and government offices were disrupted, and some firms reportedly went back to fax machines to confirm trades.

I don’t think the answer is to stop standardizing on good tools, since that’s usually what makes operations cheaper and faster. But it does mean that when one of those tools fails, it takes a lot down with it, and most teams haven’t thought much about what they’d do in that moment.

A few questions I’d ask any operations team this week: 
- Which single vendor, if it went dark for 24 hours, would stop revenue? 
- Does anyone know the manual fallback, and has anyone actually practiced it? 
- And is that dependency written down anywhere, or just assumed?

The Fed’s framing for the day was “connect and protect,” and I came away thinking most of us have put far more effort into the first part than the second.

We had APIs that were easier to use, we cared a lot about the quality of the product and uptime, and we spent a ton of time in the fintech ecosystem. We were so much closer to the ecosystem than our competitors, and as fintech grew, Plaid grew. And eventually we built more specialized APIs and network effects (moats!), and started going after the incumbents' user base.

I remember we used to host events at the Plaid office where we invited founders of all these companies once a month. It was a who's who of fintech. It was really cool to be in the middle of all that innovation. 

So when people ask how Plaid won despite not being the first mover, that's how I think about it.

If you're building a platform, you don't need to win the customers who are the biggest today. You want to figure out who the next generation of winners will be, and get them building on you early.

If you're right about that wave of innovation, you can ride it for a very long time.

🎯 What if being right about the future is not enough to make a good investment?

Silicon Valley is built on the belief that the next big opportunity is always around the corner. But recognizing a promising technology and making a successful investment in it are two very different things.

During our Canadian Executive MBA Silicon Valley mission, we met Michael Liou, an investor and startup advisor with experience spanning more than 190 startups, including SpaceX, Robinhood and Zapier.

One of his messages was surprisingly simple: “Boring is underrated.”

What made this particularly interesting was his explanation of how investment decisions can be influenced by FOMO, inflated valuations and confirmation bias.

And there is another layer to this. Venture capital funds themselves face pressure to deploy capital, generate returns and raise their next funds. In other words, even professional investors operate within structures that can influence their decisions.

This becomes especially relevant in today’s AI investment boom.

Michael highlighted the enormous capital flowing into AI infrastructure, while questions remain about monetization, sustainable competitive advantages and the economics behind some of the most ambitious valuations.

It raises an interesting question: Can you be completely right about a technology’s potential and still be wrong about investing in it?

I think you can.

A technology can transform an entire industry without every company developing it becoming a successful business. And even a successful business may not justify the price investors are willing to pay.

Perhaps that is what makes Michael’s observation about boring investments so relevant. The real challenge is not simply identifying what could change the world, but understanding where sustainable value will actually be created, and how much of that value is already reflected in the price.

A valuable reminder that good investment decisions require not only vision, but also discipline and independent judgment. 🧠

📘 Transformation Tuesday | From the Bo | Your AI Business Case Promises Efficiency. But Where Is the Business Value?

Imagine your organization implements an AI-powered contract management application.

Contract review time decreases by 40%.

The implementation team celebrates.

Leadership sees an impressive productivity improvement.

But where is the business value?

Did the organization reduce operating costs?

Did procurement negotiate better contract terms?

Were contractual risks identified earlier?

Did employees use their additional capacity to deliver more strategic work?

Or did everyone simply complete the same work faster?

Time saved does not automatically translate into financial value.

AI can create benefits beyond efficiency, including improved decisions, reduced supplier risk, and stronger supply chain resilience.

But these outcomes must be defined and measured.

In Chapter 9 of my book, The Impact of AI in Supply Management: The Rise of Intelligent Procurement, I explore why an AI business case must go beyond traditional cost savings to demonstrate measurable financial and strategic value.

💡 3 Takeaways

1️⃣ Measure business outcomes, not just productivity.

Identify how AI should improve cost, risk, quality, compliance, or operational performance.

2️⃣ Establish a baseline before implementation.

Document current cycle times, costs, error rates, and performance so improvements can be measured.

3️⃣ Explain how efficiency creates value.

Determine whether time savings will reduce expenses, increase capacity, improve decisions, or support additional strategic activities.

AI making procurement faster is an operational improvement.

AI making procurement more valuable is a business transformation.

Are your AI business cases measuring the difference?

I’ve had the privilege of working again with Barry Rogers through the Pracademic Lab, and sponsoring a dissertation by MSc student Devon Litherland exploring a question that feels increasingly important for organisations: why AI adoption is far more than a technology challenge?
  
One of the things I love about this collaboration is exactly what the Pracademic Lab is trying to create - a closer connection between academic rigour and the messy realities of organisational life.
  
And that feels particularly important right now.
  
The world of work is changing at extraordinary speed. Leaders are being asked to make decisions about AI, skills, jobs, leadership and the future of their organisations while many of the answers are still emerging. Bringing academic thinking closer to practice - and practice closer to academic thinking - can help us ask better questions and navigate that uncertainty with a little more depth.
 
Devon’s research surfaced some fascinating tensions: AI can increase productivity while people hide how they are using it; it can accelerate output while potentially changing how people develop judgement and expertise; and leaders are being asked to guide others through a transition they are still navigating themselves.

American Bureau of Shipping (ABS), bringing classification, technical and regulatory expertise.

@Prologis Ventures, the investment arm of one of the world’s largest logistics real estate companies.

IINO Lines Gulf DMCC , bringing shipping operations, industry knowledge and access to real-world applications.

1. Industrial #autonomy and operational resilience.
2. #AI-driven operational decision-making.
3. Robotics and #automation.
4. #Energy #transition and next-generation #fuels.
5. Maritime and dual-use #technologies.

It has already made three investments, including Quartermaster, a US startup developing shipboard #sensor technology to map ocean conditions and vessel movements. Quartermaster subsequently raised a US$43 million Series A, co-led by First Round Capital and Quiet Capital.



Should traditional shipowners invest in tech?

➖A global #logistics #property group with visibility across ports, warehouses and supply chains.

Some big personal news 😅 I am thrilled to announce that I have GONE BACK TO OPERATING!!! 

After co-leading StandUp Ventures' investment in GridBank’s oversubscribed $6M seed round alongside Version One Ventures and GreenSky Ventures earlier this year, I decided to take the leap and formally join the incredible founder Laura Lalonde as her Director of Product. 

First, StandUp Ventures. Venture is built on pattern matching, but there’s a problem. The founders venture has historically backed aren’t a representative sample of the people capable of building extraordinary companies. They’re the people given a chance to try with capital behind them. This matters even more as AI moves to the top of the funnel. Train it on who got funded before and it’ll screen out the very outliers we’re supposed to be finding. That makes capital harder to access, and it costs investors alpha.

Working on that problem at StandUp Ventures inspired me deeply for 6 years. I have endless gratitude for Michelle McBane, Lucas Perlman, our LPs, and every founder who let me learn alongside them. I can’t wait to see what StandUp Ventures does next.

I come by my conviction honestly. My grandfather never treated being a woman as a reason to expect any less of me. Growing up, I’d show up at his sunroom door every morning at 8 a.m. An accomplished real estate developer, repeat entrepreneur, and investor, he spent thousands of hours with me, critiquing my businesses, probing what I thought about the decisions he was making, and asking what I really wanted to do with my life. 

More than anything, he believed in human agency. That people were capable of more than they thought and deserved the chance to find out. And that sometimes opportunity is nothing more than someone who believes when it changes what you think is possible for yourself.

He died late October. I found out at SFO, on my way home from a trip with Laura in the photo below. So much of the confidence behind this leap is his.

Now, GridBank. I have no interest in building the future where machines replace people. Rather, I know that humanity possesses inherent and permanent economic value. Even as machines get more capable, people have access to information machines require. What you see because you’re there. What you know because you lived through it. What you're about to do next. This proximity to reality becomes more valuable as intelligence gets cheaper. The question is whether we build an economy in which people can contribute what they know and share in the value it creates.

At GridBank, we’re building the way to ask the world a question and compensate the humans with the answer. 

I believe we can make the world better doing this, and I can’t think of anyone I’d rather build it with than the visionary, values-driven, headstrong, hilarious Laura Lalonde.

I’ll write more about my grandfather, my time investing, and about all of this, when I have the words. 

For now, I’m really happy to be building again.  😊

I’m now two years into actively deploying capital, with 17 investments made. One stat that really struck me is that 11 of those 17 companies have at least one woman founder. That’s well above the industry average: PitchBook’s 2025 report found that about 24% of US venture deals went to companies with at least one woman founder. 

This isn’t something I planned. My focus has always been to invest in the best people and companies working on massive problems, but I still wanted to understand why my numbers look so different from the industry’s.
 
So I looked further upstream and analyzed my entire pipeline. I had about 763 companies recorded. (Side note: this means I’ve invested in only about 2% of the companies I’ve seen, and even that might be underestimating 😓) About 38% of my pipeline had at least one woman co-founder. For comparison, the EIT’s study of European deep tech startups found that about 24% of those founded in 2022 had a woman on the founding team. In my own funnel, that share went up at every stage, to about half of the companies I took first meetings with and 70% of those that reached deeper diligence.
 
I ask every founder the same questions. Why are you and your team uniquely positioned to build this startup? What customer traction do you have so far? How do you plan to scale this economically? Since every founder gets the same questions, my best guess is that a lot of it comes down to who reaches me in the first place, through the communities and networks I’m part of. Either way, I’m certain the top of the funnel in deep tech could be better. I’d love to hear how other early-stage investors track this.

Over the last few years, I’ve sat through a lot of startup pitches.
  
Demo Days with 80+ startups, multiple editions of Smart India Hackathon as a jury member, along with a recent cohort evaluation with 30 founders, and countless one-on-one conversations with students who had "just an idea".
  
Somewhere along the way, I stopped being impressed by good slides.
  
What I notice now is how a founder reacts when someone pokes a hole in their plan.
  
Some get defensive. Some go quiet and take notes. Some challenge the question itself. And some genuinely try to understand what they might have missed.
  
Interestingly, the second and third groups are often the ones worth watching.
  
I think that's because a pitch is rehearsed, but a difficult question isn't.
  
When someone asks, "What if your biggest customer says no?" or "Why would someone pay for this when an alternative already exists?", you quickly find out how much thinking has actually gone into the business.
  
I've seen founders with five-slide decks answer those questions beautifully, and founders with 40-slide presentations struggle to find an answer.
  
It has changed how I give feedback, too.
  
I used to start by pointing out what was wrong with a business plan. Now, I prefer to start by asking:
  
"What have you actually tested so far?"
  
Because the answer tells me where a founder really stands, far better than any pitch deck can.
  
And perhaps that's one of the most underrated qualities of a founder: the willingness to question their own assumptions before someone else does.
  
Over the coming weeks, I'll be sharing more observations from the other side of the startup ecosystem, from pitch days and funding programs to founder conversations and the lessons that rarely make it into a presentation.
  
A question for founders and aspiring entrepreneurs here:
  
If someone challenged one assumption in your business today, which one would be hardest for you to defend?
  
Drop it in the comments. Let's have an honest conversation.
  
And if you're building something, I'd genuinely love to hear about it. What are you working on?

Building a Business Is More Than Tracking Numbers.

One important lesson in business leadership is that an early-stage business cannot be managed only through numbers, reports and trackers.

Before expecting consistent results, we must build the foundation that makes those results possible.

This requires:

- Market Understanding: Listening to the ground and understanding real market challenges.
- Distribution Development: Building strong distribution networks and wholesale partnerships.
- Execution Excellence: Investing in field capabilities, market activation and consumer engagement.
- Performance Management: Establishing meaningful KPIs that measure progress and drive accountability.

Numbers are essential. Trackers are necessary. But they should support business development, not replace it.

Especially in emerging markets, leadership requires the ability to balance data-driven decisions with practical market realities.

My leadership philosophy: Build the market, strengthen execution, measure progress and deliver sustainable growth.

Because ultimately, our objective should not simply be to report business performance, but to create the conditions that generate it.

DRIVE GROWTH

Sales Leadership | Performance | Business Development

Growth is not something you demand from a sales team. It is something you build into the way that team operates.

Organizations often measure sales success through revenue, quotas, pipeline volume, and closed deals. These metrics matter. But they tell us what happened—not necessarily what created sustainable growth.

The real question leaders should ask is:

Are we developing salespeople who can consistently create value, or are we simply pressuring them to produce results?

Five Principles for Driving Sustainable Sales Growth

1. Sell Business Outcomes, Not Products

Customers rarely invest in a solution simply because of its features. They invest because they need to solve a problem, reduce risk, improve efficiency, or prepare for future demand.

The strongest sales professionals connect their recommendations to measurable business outcomes.

2. Replace Transactional Selling With Consultative Discovery

A salesperson who talks the most doesn’t necessarily create the most value.

Ask better questions. Understand operational challenges. Identify the cost of inaction. Discover what the customer is trying to accomplish before recommending a solution.

3. Build Pipeline Quality, Not Just Quantity

A large pipeline can create the illusion of momentum.

Real pipeline strength comes from qualified opportunities, meaningful buyer engagement, credible timelines, and clearly defined next steps.

Activity is important. Progress is what matters.

4. Turn Sales Training Into a Competitive Advantage

Training should extend beyond memorizing product specifications and rehearsing objection-handling scripts.

Develop critical thinking, financial understanding, negotiation skills, industry knowledge, and the ability to communicate with decision-makers.

A trained salesperson explains the product. A developed sales professional explains the business impact.

5. Lead With Accountability and Continuous Improvement

High-performing sales cultures balance expectations with development.

Measure conversion rates, opportunity progression, customer retention, and revenue quality—not simply the number of calls made.

Coach behaviors that produce stronger outcomes rather than rewarding activity alone.

The Leadership Perspective

Sustainable growth happens when three elements work together:

People + Process + Customer Value = Scalable Growth

A business cannot consistently outperform the capabilities of the people responsible for developing its customer relationships.

Sales leadership is not merely about pushing a team to close more deals.

It is about building the judgment, discipline, confidence, and commercial understanding required to create opportunities that competitors overlook.

The ultimate measure of a sales professional is not simply how much they sell—but how much value they create in the process.

A Question for Sales Leaders

Are we training our teams to meet this month’s quota, or developing professionals capable of driving growth for the next five years?

Persuasion vs Manipulation — The Line That Matters💥
There is a line in sales that separates the profession from the predatory.
It is not always obvious. But it is always important.🚫
The difference between persuasion and manipulation is not the technique.
💫It is the intent.
🔹Persuasion: I understand what you genuinely need, and I am using everything I know about communication and psychology to help you see whether what I offer genuinely serves that need.

🔹Manipulation: I am using what I know about your psychological vulnerabilities to get you to a yes that primarily serves my outcome regardless of whether it serves yours.

🚫The same language pattern can be either, depending on who is using it and why.

This is why I am deeply invested in how sales psychology is taught.

When NLP-based influence techniques are taught without ethical grounding, they become tools of pressure.

When they are taught with a clear commitment to the client's genuine best interest, they become the most effective form of authentic communication available.

The most sustainable sales careers are built on a reputation for helping people make decisions that were genuinely right for them.

That reputation compounds over years.
Manipulation produces short-term numbers and long-term damage to trust, both external and internal.

Where do you see the line between persuasion and manipulation in your industry?

The article "7 Golden Rules of Sales – Expanded Version" by Dean Seddon highlights seven important principles for becoming successful in sales. �
LinkedIn +1
1. Sell Results and Solutions, Not Services
Customers don't buy a product or service itself—they buy the outcome it gives them. Focus on how your product solves a problem or improves their life.
2. Speak to Customers' Needs, Wants, Fears, and Dreams
Understand what your customers truly care about. When you show that you understand their challenges and goals, they trust you more.
3. Lead with Emotion and Support It with Logic
People often make decisions emotionally and then justify them with facts. Use stories and emotions to connect with customers, then provide logical reasons to support the purchase.
4. Be Specific Instead of Trying to Appeal to Everyone
A broad message attracts nobody. Clearly define who your product is for and tailor your message to that audience.
5. Create a Sense of Urgency
People act when they feel they might miss an opportunity. Limited-time offers, exclusive deals, or limited availability can encourage customers to make decisions.
6. Show Your Personality and Be Interesting
People buy from people they know, like, and trust. Be authentic, share your experiences, and let your personality shine.
7. Build Familiarity Before Selling
Selling to strangers is difficult. Build relationships, share helpful content, and create trust before asking for the sale. Familiarity makes customers more comfortable buying from you.

Just finished reading The Psychology of Selling by Brian Tracy, and one thing became abundantly clear:

People don't buy products. They buy confidence, trust, and solutions.

Despite being written years ago, the principles are even more relevant in today's Indian sales landscape.

In India, sales isn't just about pitching features or negotiating prices. It's about understanding diverse customer mindsets, building long-term relationships, and creating value across every interaction.

Some reflections that resonated with me:

1. Relationships outperform transactions. Whether you're dealing with distributors, architects, builders, retailers, or end customers, trust remains the strongest currency.

2. Preparation creates confidence. The best sales professionals don't "wing it." They know their products, competitors, and customer pain points inside out.

3. Questions sell better than presentations. Listening carefully often uncovers opportunities that a scripted sales pitch never will.

4. Objections are buying signals. In the Indian market, price objections often hide concerns around value, service, or trust—not affordability.

5. Continuous learning is a competitive advantage. Markets evolve, customer expectations change, and only those who keep learning continue winning.

As someone working in the premium bath and wellness industry, I see these lessons play out every day. Premium products are rarely sold on specifications alone—they are sold through credibility, consultation, and customer confidence.

Brian Tracy's message is timeless:

The most valuable asset in sales isn't your product. It's the person selling it.

For every salesperson in India—from FMCG to Building Materials, SaaS to Financial Services—this book is a reminder that sales success begins with mastering human psychology before mastering sales techniques.

The buyer didn't need more information.

He needed a reason to trust the decision.
I remember a conversation where the buyer kept asking me the same question in different ways:

“Are you sure this is the right option?”

I had already explained the features.
I had answered his questions.
I had shown him the numbers.

But something was still missing.
So instead of giving him more information, I changed the conversation.

I showed him how other buyers in a similar situation had approached the same decision.

Not by saying:
“Everyone is buying this.”
That would have sounded like a sales tactic.

Instead, I explained why those buyers chose the option they did — what problem they were trying to solve, what they compared, and what mattered most to them.

The conversation changed.
He stopped asking:
“Is this the right choice?”
And started asking:

“How would this work in my situation?”
That distinction matters.
Social proof isn't about telling people what everyone else is doing.
And contrast isn't about making one option look artificially better.

Used properly, they give the buyer a clearer reference point for evaluating the decision.

Sometimes the buyer doesn't need another feature.
They need a better frame for understanding the choice.

That’s why I always ask:
What does this buyer have to compare this decision against?

I explore this psychology — along with practical frameworks, examples, and techniques — in *Your Guide to Sales Psychology*.

Have you ever noticed that something suddenly feels affordable after you've seen a more expensive option first?

I recently came across a sales concept called the Rejection-Then-Retreat Technique in Psychology of Persuasion.

The idea is simple.

You first present a bigger offer.

When that doesn't work, you step back and present the offer you actually wanted the person to consider.

For example, if you're selling a $10 watch, you might show a $20 watch first. After the buyer decides it's too expensive, the $10 watch suddenly feels like a better deal.

What's interesting is that people don't always make decisions based on price alone. Sometimes, what they saw before influences how they see what's in front of them.

Human psychology shows up in sales more often than we realize.

USDT is not a FEMA exemption. And a foreign subsidiary is not a regulatory escape route.

The ED's scrutiny of CoinDCX and Delta Exchange could be a defining moment for India's crypto and fintech ecosystem.

But the real story is much bigger than crypto.

It is about how money moves across borders, how global financial products are offered to Indian customers, and where technology ends and regulatory responsibility begins.

Three developments deserve attention:
🔹 Crypto trading: Allegations of INR being converted into USDT and routed to overseas exchanges to facilitate customer trading.
🔹 Crypto derivatives: Questions around overseas execution of futures and options, margin funding and the role of foreign group entities.
🔹 Tokenised US stocks: Are customers actually buying foreign shares, or are they taking synthetic derivative exposure linked to the prices of Apple, Google and Tesla?

And this brings us to the most important question: FEMA.

A transaction does not become permissible merely because:
- INR is converted into USDT.
- Funds move through blockchain wallets.
- An overseas subsidiary is involved.
- The product is marketed as tokenised equity.
- The platform is registered with FIU-IND.

The underlying economic transaction, the movement of value, the parties involved and the applicable regulatory permissions still matter.

There are some critical questions every fintech founder and board should be asking:
- Is the product itself permissible for Indian residents?
- Who is the actual counterparty?
- Where is the trade executed?
- Who holds customer funds and collateral?
- Is the cross-border movement of value permitted under FEMA?
- Does the overseas entity have the necessary regulatory and business justification?

My biggest takeaway for the industry:
- Regulatory compliance cannot begin after a product is launched and achieves scale.
- It must be embedded into the product architecture itself.

India's fintech ecosystem needs innovation in tokenisation, digital assets and global financial access. But innovation cannot be built on regulatory assumptions.

The next generation of successful fintech businesses will need three equally strong foundations:
Technology architecture + Financial architecture + Regulatory architecture.

Because building a product that works is one thing
Building a product that can legally operate, scale and withstand regulatory scrutiny is an entirely different challenge.

I have explored the FEMA implications, alleged transaction structures, movement of funds, ED's areas of investigation and possible regulatory pathways in my latest article.

South Africa has already seen what regulatory delay can cost.

In my earlier article, "Beyond the Hallucination: Why a Regulatory Vacuum is South Africa's Real AI Risk", I made an important connection between the country's delayed response to cryptocurrency regulation and the challenges now facing its AI regulatory framework.

One of the figures I referred to was the R63 billion in outward Bitcoin wallet volume since 1 January 2019 identified by the South African Reserve Bank - a fertile ground for cybercrime.

That figure illustrated the extent to which digital assets had developed the capacity to facilitate cross-border movements of value outside conventional financial infrastructure. The regulatory conversation has since evolved with the Standard Bank case and Mangundhla case, and illustrate why regulatory certainty matters.

Now, with the #Microsoft incident that followed the recent #Binance incident, we are confronted with another dimension of the same problem: 

What happens when digital assets are compromised in South Africa? Who bears the loss: the investor, the exchange or the state? One thing is clear, the answer cannot simply be to leave everything to the market.

We need frameworks that recognise the decentralised nature of blockchain technology while ensuring adequate accountability for private sector players.

Regulation should not be the enemy of innovation. It should be the infrastructure that allows innovation to develop sustainably.

I explore this further in the second part of the "Crypto Contradiction" article series.

In my latest article, I explore why some of the highest-performing conversion copywriters aren't necessarily the best writers—they're the ones who understand buyers the best.

I’m a salesperson, but I don’t believe my job is to sell people.

I believe my job is to serve them.

Someone comes to me because they have a problem, a gap, or something in their current process that isn’t working.

My job is to understand that problem and figure out if what I offer can genuinely help solve it.

That’s where my Christian faith shows up in the way I approach sales.

When I think about Jesus and the way He interacted with people, I think about service.

When Jesus went out to spread God’s Word and call people to believe He was the Son of God, He did it from a place of conviction, mission, and service, not from a set of tactics or techniques.

I think salespeople can learn a lot from that.

We spend so much time learning discovery frameworks, objection handling, negotiation tactics, closing techniques, and sales psychology.

And those things are valuable.

But we don’t talk enough about the heart posture behind them.

Because you can ask the perfect discovery question and still not genuinely care about the answer.

You can master objection handling and still push someone toward something that isn’t right for them.

You can follow every sales methodology perfectly and still make the conversation more about your quota than their problem.

That’s why tips and tricks alone don’t work.

The intention behind them matters.

As a sales rep, I try to see myself as a servant first.

Understand the problem.

Listen.

Tell the truth about whether I can help.

And if I can, do everything I can to solve it well.

That mindset has shaped the way I sell more than any sales technique ever has.

https://lnkd.in/guuzcAFh his sounds simple. Protect your time. But you know as a salesperson there are many ways to drift.
Salespeople rarely lose selling time all at once. Another internal email, an unnecessary meeting, an overworked proposal, or research that never turns into action. 
By Friday, everyone has been busy, but too little time has been spent face to face with customers and prospects.
That actually loses you money.
Increasing Time Spent Selling™ (face to face client time) cannot be left to good intentions.
Increasing face to face time with clients and prospective clients requires a visible, repeatable process.
Begin by establishing the truth.
For one week, have every seller track time in categories: Face-to-face selling, prospecting, preparation, travel, service work, meetings and administration. Do not use the exercise to punish. I always find it is better to reward the behaviors you want to see and avoid trying to catch people doing something wrong.
Use it to expose where the week is going. Learn from police detectives. Memory is unreliable. A written record is not.
Next, establish a face-to-face goal for every seller. The number should be challenging but realistic. Then work backward.
How many appointments must be scheduled to achieve it?
How many calls, referrals, walk-ins and follow-ups will create those appointments?
Now the team has a process instead of a wish.
Protect selling blocks on the calendar as fiercely as an important client meeting. Internal meetings should be short, purposeful and placed outside prime customer-contact hours.
Administrative work should be grouped together.
Proposals should have deadlines.
Problems that do not require the seller should be redirected.
Each morning, sellers should identify the people they intend to see.
Each afternoon, they should record what happened and schedule the next action.
Sales managers should review activity, not merely ask, “What did you sell?” 
Revenue is a lagging result.
Face-to-face activity is a leading indicator managers and sellers can influence today.
Finally, compare each week with the previous one.
Did face-to-face time increase?
If not, where did it leak away?
Remove one obstacle, tighten one habit and reset the calendar.
Small improvements compound.
The goal is not paperwork or making sellers feel watched. People hate to be watched. So, this is all about your relationship with the individual sellers.
The goal is protecting them from a workday filled with everything except selling.
